#2072. Newcastle United Women’s team turn on the style at St James’ Park in another step to the title

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Newcastle United Women’s team faced their Burnley counterparts at St James’ Park on Sunday in this important second tier league match.

With Soffia Kelly’s two week emergency loan spell having ended with the Newcastle United Women’s team, she returned to parent club Aston Villa this week.

In her place came Anna Pederson from Charlton on a one week deal which suggests first choice goalie Anna Tamminen is close to a return.

Beth Lumsden and Martha Thomas have been nominated for October’s WSL 2 Player of the Month award. They face opposition from Ipswich’s Princess Ademiluyi, Elise Hughes of Sunderland, Leticia McKenna of Nottingham Forest and Watford’s Phoebie Poole.

The club have appointed Sarah Lowden as Academy Manager. She arrives from the FA where she spent the past seven years working in a variety of roles developing young players. Although Sarah is from the area she previously worked with academies at Reading and Burton Albion.

“I’m excited to play a key role in the development of the next generation of talented footballers, helping them fulfil their potential both on and off the pitch, while contributing to the continued growth and success of the women’s game at this incredible club.” She said on joining.

Before kick-off there was a minute’s silence for Remembrance Sunday. Female military officers laid a poppy wreath at the centre circle and were led out by Sophie Akrill, who along with serving her country plays football locally for Cullercoats and ice hockey for Whitley Bay Beacons.

Newcastle manager Tanya Oxtoby made just one change from last week, Hungarian central defender Hanna Németh coming in to start her first WSL 2 game, as they lined up in their usual 4-3-3 formation. Burnley went with five at the back and a midfield diamond in front of them, with just a loan striker up top.

All the fans were housed in the East Stand with both the Gallowgate and Leazes closed for this game with newly promoted Burnley.

Sensing there were goals to be had, Newcastle went for the jugular from the off. They nearly took the lead very early on but Jordan Nobbs fired well over from 12 yards after meeting a cutback from the left. Then a cross from the left by Nobbs was deflected over to striker Kathleen McGovern, who couldn’t quite bundle the ball home from point-blank range.

But a minute later the Scottish striker made amends and fired the Lasses into a lead they wouldn’t relinquish. Some neat build up play saw the ball laid back to Lois Joel on the edge of the area, who curled a pass to the back post for McGovern to fire home. The former Hibernian forward seems to love playing against Burnley after she netted a hat-trick against them in a pre-season game at Gateshead earlier in the campaign.

Newcastle were relentless in their pursuit for goals and quickly doubled their lead soon after. Beth Lumsden again worked well down the right channel before creating some space close to the byline. As she tried to cut the ball back for a team mate, former Lasses defender Deanna Cooper appeared to slice at the ball and redirected it past goalie Kirstie Levell.

Ironically it was Cooper’s third goal for Newcastle at St James’ Park, after netting a last minute equaliser against Southampton two seasons ago, and then also finding the net against Sunderland.

The Lady Mags could have added to their lead and perhaps should have been four or five goals to the good before the break. Kaitlyn Torpey found Martha Thomas, whose first-time lay-off to Jordan Nobbs opened up space for a curled effort towards the bottom corner, but she was denied by a stunning save by Levell. Before Thomas headed well wide with another chance three minutes later.

Then as half-time approached, a loose ball in the box fell to midfielder Katie Bradley, who found space between the Burnley defenders but could only stab it around the outside of the foot of the post after Levell had punched McGovern’s cross clear. Newcastle looked certain to add a third on the stroke of half-time but Alethea Paul produced an excellent block to deny Nobbs.

Burnley failed to test Newcastle, and goalie Kayla Rendell could have literally put her feet up and read the newspaper throughout the game, she had so little to do.

However, in Alethea Paul and Emma Siddall they had two very willing runners at wing back and veteran former Manchester United striker Rachel Williams battling away with a physical presence up front.

They threatened for the first time in the 37th minute when Paul’s inswinging corner was met by Williams, but the forward could only direct her header over the bar.

Perhaps Burnley’s best chance came when Siddall advanced well down the right flank leaving the Newcastle defence flat footed. But despite getting in behind the home side’s back four, she was unable to get her strike on target. Her effort sailing over the crossbar.

Charlie Chadwick made a difference when she came on to play on the left of midfield, firing wide from 20 yards soon after arriving.

But Newcastle made it three with half an hour to go when Lumsden charged towards goal once again before finding league top scorer Martha Thomas who controlled well before finding the net at the Gallowgate end from six yards out.

A flurry of substitutions saw some of the rhythm go out the game with a whole new front three up top for the lasses. However, Freya Gregory did star in her 25 minute cameo as she had a couple of efforts that narrowly cleared the bar.

Tyler Toland deflected a couple of Newcastle shots, before Levell produced another fine stop to keep out a fierce angled drive from Gregory. Then Jessie Gale, also on and playing up top, squandered an opportunity to make it four, failing to connect with Gregory’s cross.

Burnley then suffered a further setback when Charley Docherty, who had been on the pitch for just 20 minutes, limped off with an apparent hamstring injury. The Clarets, who only had five outfield players named on their bench, had to play on with ten players after they had already used up all their allocated substitutions.

Nobbs, who started Newcastle off on the right track, had the final say when she forced a comfortable save from Levell in the closing stages. While Cooper produced a crucial block to deny McLaughlan from close range as Newcastle saw out the victory.

Newcastle United: Kayla Rendell, Rachel McLauchlan (c), Hanna Németh, Gemma Evans, Kaitlyn Torpey, Katie Bradley (Mollie Lambert 63), Lois Joel, Jordan, Nobbs, Beth Lumsden (Oona Sevenius 69), Martha Thomas (Jessie Gale 69), Kathleen McGovern (Beth Lumsden Freya Gregory 63).

Subs not used: Anna Pedersen, Charlotte Wardlaw, Jemma Purfield, Hildur Antonsdóttir, Aoife Mannion.

Burnley: Kirstie Levell, Emma Siddall, Jessica Hennessy, Deanna Cooper, Naomi Hartley (Charley Docherty 65), Alethea Paul, Brenna McPartlan, Tyler Toland, Jamie Finn (Charlie Chadwick 55), Christie Harrison-Murray, Rachel Williams (Brooke Cairns 80).

Subs not used: Jackie Burns, Kiera Sena, Maddi Wilde.

Where that leaves Newcastle United Women’s team

Newcastle remain unbeaten in WSL2 and have a three point cushion over second placed Sunderland after the Lady Black Cats won the River Wear derby in Durham. Elsewhere, Ipswich finally lost their unbeaten start to the season after they slipped up to an in-form Bristol City.

There are 15 league games remaining with only top spot good enough for automatic promotion to the top flight this season.

Teams that finish second and third will play off for the right to face the team that finishes second bottom of WSL1 and a chance at promotion, although that represents a much tougher route.

Newcastle travel to the Stadium of Light for next Sunday’s top of the table clash with Sunderland. The Lasses have already faced their local rivals once this season and lost 1-0 at Gateshead in the League Cup so they will be looking to put things right this time in the league encounter.

United are next at home the following Sunday when they host Nottingham Forest in a League Cup group game at Gateshead International Stadium.

#2071. GdS: A combined salary less than Ramos’ – the story behind the Ferencvaros ‘miracle’

AC Milan’s opponents Ferencvaros are one of a few teams to have a perfect record in the Europa League, and their story is a fascinating one.

Ferencváros arrive at San Siro having won all three of their league phase games thus far. In addition to that, they are 20 unbeaten across all competitions and they will go top of their domestic league if they win their game in hand. La Gazzetta dello Sport (seen below) share some insight on the Hungarians.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Gonçalo Ramos’s gross salary €12.8m (€7m net including bonuses) is equivalent to the entire wage bill of Ferencváros. The combined salaries of the Hungarian club’s players total €11m.

Their highest earner is Naby Keïta, who accepted a contract worth just over €1.2m gross per season, seeking a career resurgence at the club with the largest payroll in the Hungarian league.

The Serbian midfielder Birmančević – formerly of Sparta Prague and Getafe, who arrived last summer – earns a slightly lower salary. Meanwhile, attacking midfielder Zachariassen earns around €700k and has scored three goals so far, as has Alphadjo Cissé.

In terms of wages, therefore, there is simply no comparison between the Rossoneri and Ferencváros. Yet, the Hungarians have won every match, while Milan have only three points. All the more reason not to take them lightly.

Gabor Kubatov has been on the board of Ferencváros since 2010, becoming president a year later. Under his leadership, the club has won eight Hungarian league titles. His personal history is quite unique: as a young man, he was a regular in ‘Sector 2’ – the section occupied by the ultras.

He later changed paths, and in 2006, he became a member of parliament, representing Fidesz, the party of Viktor Orbán. Despite his own background in the stands, his relationship with the Ferencváros ultras has not always been smooth.

In 2014, in an effort to combat violence and incidents of racism, Kubatov introduced a biometric identification system for stadium entry. A segment of the most ardent supporters responded by boycotting home matches, a protest that lasted for over three years.

An agreement was finally reached and the fans returned to the stands. With their support, Ferencváros went on to win seven consecutive league titles.

On 10 December 2017, a young Adam Nagy faced Milan while playing for Bologna. It didn’t go well: a 2-1 victory for the Rossoneri. Today, Nagy returns as a far more mature leader of his ‘miracle’ Ferencváros side.

Indeed, a significant portion of the Hungarian midfielder’s career has unfolded in Italy. He spent three years with the Rossoblù from 2016 to 2019 – following his initial breakthrough at Ferencváros – before returning to Italy in 2021 to join Pisa, having previously left to try his hand at Bristol City in England.

His most recent stint was with Spezia, which he departed this summer to return to his homeland. Yesterday, in a press conference, Rúben Amorim spoke very highly of him: “He is very skilled in the initial phase of build-up play.”

His ability to circulate the ball deep in his own half is his greatest strength. Conversely, he rarely ventures into the final third. The proof? Throughout all his years in Italy, he scored only one goal: against Verona in Serie A.

From the European champions Liverpool to Ferencvaros. Naby Keita – who will start on the bench tonight, hasn’t had the career he hoped for. Liverpool paid €65m to sign him from RB Leipzig in 2018, he won six more trophies in addition to the Champions League with Klopp’s English side.

In 2023, the Guinean midfielder moved to Werder Bremen, where he was left out of the squad after refusing to travel for the trip to Leverkusen because he wouldn’t have been a starter. Since January 2025, he has been at Ferencváros, who acquired him a year later.

Wearing a Liverpool shirt, Keïta has already beaten Milan at San Siro on 7 December 2021, a defeat that contributed to the Diavolo being eliminated in the group stage.

A less pleasant memory for Keïta involves his encounter with Luka Modrić when he came on in the final minutes of the 2022 Champions League final, which Liverpool lost to Real Madrid.

#2070. Player Ratings: Blackburn 2-1 West Ham as Hermansen Has a Nightmare

West Ham’s promising start at Ewood Park ultimately counted for very little as Scott Parker’s side slipped to a 2-1 defeat against Blackburn Rovers. Despite enjoying plenty of possession and creating opportunities, the Hammers were undone by poor defending and some particularly questionable goalkeeping.

Joël Piroe’s late goal gave West Ham a chance of rescuing something, but the longer the game went on, the worse we seemed to play. There were some decent individual performances, particularly early on, but others will want to forget this afternoon in a hurry.

A really poor afternoon for the goalkeeper. I thought he could have been far more commanding for Blackburn’s opening goal, whether that meant catching the cross, punching it or simply getting something on the ball. He did make a straightforward late save from Todd Cantwell, but that doesn’t change my overall assessment.

One of West Ham’s more reliable performers before being substituted. Made some useful defensive interceptions and regularly pushed forward to support Bowen down the right. Tried a couple of long throws into the penalty area, although they didn’t really cause Blackburn much trouble.

Had some positive moments going forward, including a driving run from defence and a header that went narrowly wide early in the second half. However, I thought he could have done better for Blackburn’s first goal, and his performance deteriorated badly towards the end. Was fortunate not to concede a penalty before slipping twice during a dreadful passage of play that handed Blackburn a dangerous counter-attack.

Probably West Ham’s most dependable defender on the day. Made several important interceptions, particularly down the left where Blackburn repeatedly threatened, and was willing to carry the ball forward to help build attacks. Also produced a decent cross for Castellanos, although the resulting header went wide.

A mixed afternoon for the youngster. I was impressed with his willingness to get forward, his passing combinations with Austbø and some of the crosses he delivered. However, Blackburn repeatedly targeted his side, often leaving him facing two opponents, and he was beaten too easily in the build-up to the opening goal. Still very much learning the position.

Didn’t think he had a particularly good game. Had plenty of involvement, took the corners and got himself into shooting positions, but too often the final product was disappointing. Lost possession unnecessarily on occasions, failed to close down Blackburn’s second goalscorer quickly enough and wasted a promising late free kick with poor delivery.

You certainly couldn’t fault his work rate. At times he seemed to be everywhere, covering at left-back, appearing on the right and getting forward to support the attack. However, he wasn’t nearly as influential on the ball as he had been during the second half against Cardiff, and his shooting was disappointing. Replaced by Castellanos after 64 minutes.

One of West Ham’s more inventive players, particularly during the first half. Looked to move the ball quickly, attempted some clever through passes and wasn’t afraid to shoot, forcing one save and seeing another effort deflected behind. Not everything worked, but at least he was trying to make things happen.

I was genuinely surprised when he was substituted because he’d been one of West Ham’s livelier attacking players. Produced a lovely dribble past two defenders in the first half, linked up well with Mayers and delivered an excellent cross that Bowen headed against the post. Could perhaps have offered Mayers more defensive protection before Blackburn’s opener, but I thought he was contributing plenty going forward.

Blackburn 2-1 West Ham: Austbo was one of the Hammers better players

Worked hard to make things happen and was heavily involved in West Ham’s attacking play, particularly from the right. Unlucky to see his header strike the post following Austbø’s cross, while a difficult chance from close range went wide as he was falling and sliding. Also produced a lovely chipped delivery for Souček’s late header, but couldn’t quite provide the decisive contribution West Ham needed.

A frustrating performance rescued to some extent by an excellent goal. Too often he seemed hesitant in promising positions, allowing defenders to recover, while one particularly poor pass in the second half wasted a good attacking opportunity. However, he reacted brilliantly to Castellanos’ cross in the 82nd minute, firing high into the roof of the net. Whatever else you say about his performance, he took that chance extremely well.

Replaced Austbø after 58 minutes and was practically anonymous. Considering how involved Austbø had been, the substitution certainly didn’t improve West Ham’s attacking threat down the left.

Introduced for Kanté after 64 minutes and provided the cross that led to Piroe’s goal. Also had a header go wide from a Kilman delivery and was involved in the scramble that presented Bowen with a difficult chance. At least contributed something tangible to the attack.

Didn’t have a great deal of time to influence proceedings, particularly with West Ham having already lost their shape. Played one very silly ball into Orford inside our own penalty area, creating unnecessary danger. However, he also got into one of those familiar goalscoring positions in stoppage time, only to direct his header straight at the goalkeeper from Bowen’s excellent delivery.

Another substitute who came into a team that had lost its shape and was struggling for confidence. Was put in a difficult position by Souček’s poor pass inside the penalty area and was fortunate not to concede a penalty. Difficult to judge him too harshly given the limited time he had on the pitch and the state of the game when he entered.

#2069. Euro round-up: Barcelona fightback sinks Atletico Madrid as Inter Milan march on

A double from Fermin Lopez saw Barcelona come from behind to defeat Atletico Madrid 2-1 and restore their three-point lead at the top of LaLiga.

Real Madrid had drawn level with their rivals by beating Valencia on Saturday and it appeared Atletico might be the ones heading into the international break on top after Giuliano Simeone gave them a deserved early lead.

But Lopez equalised just before half-time and scored what proved to be the winner in the 66th minute as Barca cleared a major hurdle.

In Serie A, Inter Milan brought Como crashing down to earth as first-half goals from Pio Esposito and Marcus Thuram earned them a 2-0 home win.

Como continued their remarkable debut season in Europe on Wednesday by thrashing Lens 9-1, but Cesc Fabregas’ side turned in a lacklustre display at San Siro as their six-game winning run in all competitions was halted.

The victory means Inter are only one point behind leaders Lazio, who drew 1-1 away to Napoli.

Falkirk sweat over ‘big player’ after injury mars Hearts rout

Aberdeen 'set' to sack Stephen Robinson as axe looms at Pittodrie

Michael Carrick answers Man Utd quit question as crisis hits alarming new low

The Rome side remain unbeaten after nine matches, despite an own goal from Alfonso Pedraza in the second half. That came after Davide Frattesi had scored a first-half goal to put the visitors ahead.

AC Milan are up to fourth place after beating Genoa 2-1, with Alphadjo Cisse and Christian Pulisic scoring the goals inside the first 20 minutes.

Equalisers from Nick Woltemade and Gleison Bremer earned Juventus a 2-2 draw against Fiorentina.

Lille remain two points behind Ligue 1 leaders Paris Saint-Germain after beating Rennes 2-1, while Monaco were denied victory against Le Mans after a 90th-minute equaliser from Erwan Colas.

Lens’ week did not improve, with Marseille claiming a late winner in a 2-1 victory.

In the Bundesliga, Freiburg climbed to third with a 2-0 win over struggling Union Berlin, while Bayer Leverkusen were 2-1 winners away at Cologne.

THERE was an ironic cheer from the West Ham away supporters at about 88 minutes, which considering their team was 2- 1 down and looking clueless was even more remarkable.

The cheer was for Mads Hermansen finally making a save, with a shot hit straight at him being pretty much the first time he’d connected with anything, as another two goals had found their way under and past the hapless Dane.

7000 West Ham fans had made the trip to Blackburn in expectation of a triumphant start to Parker’s era and yet saw their starting eleven dominate the ball but fail to score. Hermansen had dealt with a smattering of booing from his own fans ever since Rovers took the lead with a header that went between the Dane’s legs.

Times’ up, Mads. The big concern was that Scott Parker picked him ahead of Areola. We told him….

Hardly a confidence boost for the young keeper who surely should not have been selected in the first place.

No criticism through could be attached to Hermansen for Blackburn’s second goal but West Ham found themselves two goals behind, chasing the game and seemingly nothing to offer, back passing and fiddling around in the last few minutes.

Parker can have no excuse now for continuing to select his hapless keeper. The Dane plays as if he’s got arthritic knees (take it fromm one who knows) and doesn’t dive for anything, just collapsing to the left or right, week after week.

Whatever issue there may be with second-in-line Alphonse Areola, he simply has to start after the international break.

Otherwise, we may as well simply drape a goal keeper’s jersey on the cross bar: It’ll be about as effective.

The most frustrating thing? We called this, as did just about every West Ham fan: Hermansen is just not good enough.

#2067. Hearts crisis or just a bad week, is Vrancken in trouble and has Jamestown failed?

Welcome to The Burning Questions, our new daily debate where we take one major subject in Scottish sport and tackle the three questions everyone is talking about.

Each day, our writers will offer their verdicts on the biggest issues and arguments dominating the agenda. Hearts are generating plenty of debate currently, among their own supporters and rivals, after a miserable week for them despite a promising enough start to the season prior to that.

Defeat to archenemies Hibs in a Premier Sports Cup semi-final was bad enough, but they followed it up by losing 3-1 to FC Thun (ninth in the Swiss League) in the Conference League, and it could have been more that night. Yesterday, they were four goals down to Falkirk by half-time and lost 5-2 in the end. That certainly should not be happening at Tynecastle.

Fans are frustrated and some are already questioning the management of Wouter Vrancken after the Belgian's summer arrival. They are now also questioning the club's recruitment partner, Jamestown Analytics, after the failure of many of their summer signings to hit the ground running. Sporting director Graeme Jones is also in the firing line as a result of this.

They have been dealing with a ridiculous amount of injuries, particularly in defence and midfield, but many do not feel that is enough of a mitigating factor to excuse the form.

Matthew Lindsay and Blair Meikle give their answers to today’s three Burning Questions.

Some Hearts fans are starting to turn against Wouter Vrancken after recent results. Do you think that's fair or should he still have credit in the bank from earlier in the season?

Matthew Lindsay: As bad as the defeat to Falkirk at Tynecastle was yesterday, I think the Belgian is deserving of a little bit more understanding than he is currently receiving from a section of the Hearts support.

So many Scottish clubs have struggled to juggle European and domestic commitments over the years. With the number of injuries which the capital side have now, it is asking a lot of them to successfully negotiate their hectic schedule.

Did the mentally and physically draining encounter with Thun in Switzerland on Thursday night affect their performance this weekend? Few managers in the country would have been as grateful to get to the international break as Vrancken.

He has been a victim of his own success in some respects. His predecessors Robbie Neilson, Steven Naismith and Neil Critchley all struggled to fight on more than one front.

That said, after one win in eight, he desperately needs to get back to winning ways against Dundee away on Saturday, November 21.

Aberdeen 'set' to sack Stephen Robinson as axe looms at Pittodrie Robinson on the brink but Aberdeen’s deep-rooted problems go far beyond the manager

Blair Meikle: It is far, far too early to be turning on the head coach. Hearts currently sit fourth in the table and would jump back to third if they can win their game in hand - that is nowhere near a disaster or an endgame scenario. There were positive signs before all of the injuries and it is only around a month since fans were sharing clips and waxing lyrical about the football being played.

Despite all of that, there have been worrying signs in the last week in particular. Most notably the team being too vulnerable on the counter-attack, and conceding the same sort of goals over and over.

The Belgian did reference a lot of the missing players being ones who have "tactical awareness", so their return is something that could help with that.

However, Hearts have three very tough games after the international break (Dundee away, Monaco home, Celtic home) so another three negative results will really pile the pressure on.

The injuries decimating Hearts' squad have been well documented. To what extent can they be used as an excuse for the recent run, or should they be doing better even with the players available to them?

Matthew Lindsay: I think not having Craig Halkett, Harry Milne, Tom Renaud, Blair Spittal, Calvin Miller, Oisin McEntee, Christian Borchgrevink, Rogers Mato, Tomas Magnusson and Eduardo Ageu is a reasonable excuse for Hearts’ slump in form.

At the same time, I do think that Vrancken has to shoulder much of the responsibility for the displays. His tactics were naïve in the 7-1 defeat to Celtic at Parkhead. He could be given a pass for that debacle given that it was his first game in the East End of Glasgow. But shipping five to Falkirk at home is unforgivable.

Can his team produce the sort of fluid and expansive play that he favours when they are missing so many key men? He perhaps need to be a little bit more pragmatic in his current predicament.

Blair Meikle: The injuries cannot be ignored. I've heard a lot of people saying 'the injuries cannot be an excuse' - but of course they can, to an extent. Rob any manager of 11 members of his squad, mostly starters, and performances and results will take a hit.

For example, there is no way he wants to be playing Jamie McCart at left-back, and Stuart Findlay is someone he did not appear to fancy, yet they're making up half of his back four. They are two of the players who have cost him in recent games.

All that said, the team Hearts put out yesterday should not be conceding five goals at home, especially to a team that is not Celtic or Rangers, and the manager needs to take his share of the blame for that. And his decision to play Yan Dhanda in midfield was not one I agreed with.

I think confidence is a big issue just now and a big reason why players are doing things without conviction, both in and out of possession. But you need to be made of tougher stuff to play for Hearts.

Jamestown Analytics was seen as a gamechanger when the partnership was forged but there are questions around this summer's recruitment with signings like JJ Williams, Amadou Ba-Say and others not hitting the ground running. Does this, and the form under the new manager, raise doubts about the direction of the club under this model?

Matthew Lindsay: Jamestown Analytics may have been able to pluck players like Claudio Braga and Alexandros Kyziridis from relative obscurity, but the football intelligence consultancy has certainly had its failures.

It is fair to say that JJ Williams and Amadou Ba-Say have not proved value for money to date.

Many of the players who took Hearts to the brink of the Scottish title last season, not least Stuart Findlay and Oisin McEntee, were brought in on the recommendation of then manager Derek McInnes.

But a little patience is required. It took some time for the data-driven approach which Tony Bloom introduced at Brighton down in England and Royal Union Saint-Gilloise in Belgium to bear fruit. Mistakes were made along the way and invaluable lessons were learned.

Scottish football is a unique environment and it may be a few seasons before Jamestown tunes in fully to what is required for a player to meet its demands.

Blair Meikle: Like with the head coach question, it is too early to be writing off Jamestown Analytics. Especially when the evidence of how it has worked for Brighton, Union Saint-Gilloise, Como and others is there for all to see. Why would it all of a sudden flop here?

There are massive questions over much of the recruitment in the summer. Especially because neither Williams nor Ba-Sy have been what the club needed at centre-forward and the squad has been left massively short in defensive positions. A number of the summer arrivals do not look like being successes. However, it should be pointed out that Josh McPake, Calvin Miller, Beau Reus and Tom Renaud do, while Malachi Fagan-Walcott and Laurent Mendy have shown signs despite struggling in recent weeks.

It needs to be remembered that many of the early signings Union Saint-Gilloise made with Jamestown faded into obscurity, but the Belgian side made a few trades at modest profit before slowly building things up. Hearts have made a profit on Alexandros Kyziridis and Michael Steinwender, and Claudio Braga could still be the next on the conveyor belt. Then the JTA model can start to be ramped up.

#2066. ‘They deserve it’ – Kostas Tsimikas admits familiar failing cost Liverpool in Istanbul

Kostas Tsimikas admitted that Liverpool got what they deserved in their 3-2 defeat to Fenerbahce in Istanbul on Wednesday.

The Reds were in front twice at the Sukru Saracoglu Stadium but still contrived to come away with nothing against Dirk Kuyt’s side, who claimed all three points thanks to Vedat Muriqi’s 79th-minute header.

Jeremy Jacquet was criticised for turning his back on Mason Greenwood’s free kick for the first equaliser, and Alisson Becker was culpable of poor positioning for Archie Brown’s goal to make it 2-2.

Speaking to UEFA.com after the match, Tsimikas magnanimously conceded that Fenerbahce were full value for their win and lamented Liverpool’s defending over the goals that they shipped.

The Greek defender said (via BBC Sport): “Congratulations to Fenerbahce, they deserve it. We didn’t play how we had to play. We didn’t defend after the goal we conceded. After three or four minutes, automatically we conceded another goal.

“I think we have to mark better if we want to win games. We didn’t play very good and that’s why we lost.”

It sums up how careless Liverpool were this evening that they were in the lead twice and occupied a winning position for only eight minutes against Fenerbahce, with the goals from Trey Nyoni and Alexander Isak cancelled out all too quickly.

The manner of all three goals that the home side scored will enrage Iraola – it wasn’t as though the Istanbul outfit had to produce moments of magic to inspire their way to victory over the Reds.

Tsimikas himself was far from convincing, enduring a ‘tough night’ in the words of Liverpool Echo reporter Paul Gorst as he struggled to contain the threat of Greenwood, and he ended up being substituted for Milos Kerkez with 15 minutes remaining.

Liverpool have now conceded 10 goals in their four Champions League matches, shipping three for the third European fixture in a row, a record which’ll surely concern the head coach at this phase of the competition.

The debrief from this game will not be a pleasant one, and a much better defensive performance will be required if the Reds are to return to winning ways against Crystal Palace on Sunday.

#2065. West Ham Go Full Circle as Blackburn Expose Familiar Problems

West Ham’s 2-1 defeat against Blackburn Rovers was a particularly frustrating result because, for large periods of the game, Scott Parker’s side appeared to be the better team. We started brightly, enjoyed plenty of possession and created opportunities, yet somehow managed to leave Ewood Park with nothing.

What concerns me most isn’t necessarily the result itself, although that’s bad enough. It’s the manner in which West Ham gradually deteriorated as the afternoon progressed. Even after Joël Piroe pulled a goal back late on, I thought we looked increasingly disorganised and short of confidence.

And that’s perhaps the strangest aspect of Parker’s first two matches. We started against Cardiff looking completely devoid of confidence, rediscovered it during that extraordinary second-half comeback, began confidently against Blackburn and somehow finished looking just as nervous as we had before.

I was actually quite encouraged by the opening stages. West Ham pressed high, moved the ball around reasonably well and looked determined to take the game to Blackburn. Max Kilman was particularly proactive, stepping out of defence to offer an additional passing option, while Divine Mukasa and Arne Engels were regularly involved in midfield.

Down the left, Ezra Mayers and Edvin Austbø developed a promising partnership. Mayers was willing to get forward and Austbø looked lively, producing one lovely piece of skill to beat two Blackburn players before delivering a dangerous cross.

Blackburn 2-1 West Ham: Austbo was one of the Hammers better players

However, there was a problem developing on that side of the pitch. Blackburn repeatedly managed to isolate Mayers against two opponents, and while the youngster was doing some good things offensively, he wasn’t receiving enough protection defensively.

Joël Piroe was also struggling to make the most of promising situations. On one occasion, he found himself with only a single defender to beat but hesitated for so long that three opponents eventually surrounded him. West Ham were having plenty of the ball, but Blackburn were defending deeply and making it difficult to create clear opportunities.

The second half initially offered more encouragement. Mavropanos headed narrowly wide from an Engels corner, Piroe had an effort saved and then Austbø produced an excellent cross which Bowen headed against the post. At that stage, West Ham were piling on the pressure and Blackburn were struggling to get out of their own half.

Then came the sucker punch. In the 54th minute, Blackburn broke down their right, with Mayers unable to stop the delivery into the penalty area. Andri Guðjohnsen converted, but I thought several West Ham players could have done better.

Austbø might have provided more protection for Mayers, Mavropanos could have defended the situation better and I certainly felt Mads Hermansen should have been more commanding. Whether he caught the cross, punched it or simply got something on the ball, I thought the goalkeeper had an opportunity to intervene.

It was a horrible goal to concede, particularly given how much of the attacking West Ham had been doing. Parker responded by introducing Manor Solomon for Austbø, a substitution I found surprising. The Norwegian had been one of our more involved attacking players, while Solomon subsequently struggled to make any impression.

Mohamadou Kanté was then replaced by Taty Castellanos, but West Ham were finding it increasingly difficult to establish the same attacking rhythm. Blackburn’s second goal arrived in the 71st minute, with Afolayan producing an excellent finish.

Kilman had gone down following contact to his face, but too many West Ham players appeared more interested in appealing for a foul than dealing with the danger. Engels, in particular, could have done more to close down the shot. Whatever the circumstances, you cannot simply stop defending because you believe the referee should have awarded a free kick.

At 2-0, the game appeared to be slipping away, but West Ham eventually found a route back through something remarkably straightforward. Castellanos got down the right-hand side and delivered a dangerous ball into the penalty area. Piroe reacted quickly and fired high into the roof of the net in the 82nd minute.

It was an excellent finish from a striker who, in truth, hadn’t been having a particularly good afternoon. But sometimes football really is that simple. Get the ball wide, get down the line and deliver something dangerous into the box. Give your centre-forward an opportunity to attack the ball.

Suddenly it was Blackburn 2-1 West Ham, with enough time remaining to rescue a point. Unfortunately, the expected late onslaught never really materialised. In fact, I thought West Ham became progressively worse.

Mavropanos endured a dreadful few minutes, fortunate not to concede a penalty before slipping and gifting Blackburn a counter-attack. He then slipped again while attempting to recover, while Souček subsequently played a very poor pass into Lewis Orford inside our own penalty area, creating another potentially disastrous situation.

West Ham looked increasingly nervous, and the defensive organisation seemed to disappear. There were still opportunities at both ends in stoppage time, with Todd Cantwell shooting straight at Hermansen when Blackburn might have made it 3-1.

Souček then headed directly at the Blackburn goalkeeper following an excellent chipped delivery from Bowen. It was precisely the sort of position from which we’ve seen Souček score numerous times, but once again West Ham had failed to make the most of a promising opportunity.

I keep coming back to the confidence issue because I think it explains an awful lot about what we’ve witnessed over these two matches. Against Cardiff, West Ham were absolutely dreadful during the opening 45 minutes, before producing a transformation after half-time that was almost impossible to believe.

Suddenly the players looked confident, aggressive and capable of playing some very good football. That improvement appeared to carry into the opening stages at Ewood Park, where we pressed Blackburn, moved the ball with purpose and looked considerably more comfortable in possession.

Yet by the closing stages, the confidence had completely evaporated. It was almost as though we’d gone full circle in the space of two matches, ending up precisely where we started. That is particularly disappointing because I still believe this West Ham squad possesses considerably more ability than recent performances suggest.

There were some positives. Mukasa showed invention, Austbø looked dangerous, Kilman had a decent game and Piroe took his goal extremely well. But the defensive mistakes, poor decision-making and increasingly nervous football were all too familiar.

I don’t think Scott Parker can be held responsible for everything we’ve witnessed this week. He’s barely had any meaningful time on the training pitch, and the international break offers him an opportunity to start properly implementing his ideas.

However, the evidence of these two games suggests that restoring confidence isn’t simply a matter of delivering one rousing team talk. The psychological side of West Ham’s problems may be every bit as important as the tactical side.

The frustrating thing is that we’ve already seen how much better these players can perform when they believe in themselves. Against Blackburn, we watched that belief gradually disappear again.

#2064. Hearts set for six-man injury boost as Wouter Vrancken bullish over revival

Wouter Vrancken is confident the impending return of no less than half a dozen key players from injury after the international break will help spark an upturn in fortunes for embattled Hearts.

The Jambos had 11 absentees for Sunday’s dismal 5-2 defeat at home to Falkirk and then lost key defender Malachi Fagan-Walcott in the second half.

Vrancken was optimistic that the centre-back had not sustained any serious damage and he is expecting his injury list to ease when his team return to action away to Dundee a week on Saturday.

The head coach reported that Eduardo Ageu, Tomas Magnusson, Rogers Mato, Blair Spittal, Oisin McEntee and Christian Borchgrevink are all in the frame to come back into contention, if not for Dens Park then certainly soon afterwards.

Read more: Hearts crisis or just a bad week, is Vrancken in trouble and has Jamestown failed?

“I think Eddie would be back, because he’s already training in the team,” said the head coach, offering an update on the injuries. “Tomas, for sure, because he has his protocol with the concussion.

“I think Spitts and Osh will be 50-50 when we come back. Mato, hopefully, if everything goes well.

“Christian is also maybe one who will be on the edge of coming back at this moment. I think these are the players (that are close).

“Stephen (Kingsley), we have to wait for the scan.”

Hearts have won just two of their last 11 matches amid a gruelling domestic and European schedule, leaving them fourth in the William Hill Premiership, out of the Premier Sports Cup and struggling to qualify for the Conference League knockout phase.

Vrancken is adamant that having a greater array of options available to select from will help them get back on track, however.

“I’m pretty confident in this, especially when we get numbers back, because these guys showed already what qualities and what extras they can bring on the pitch,” said the Belgian, whose side were on a nine-game unbeaten run before injuries started to undermine their campaign.

#2063. GdS: Milan’s €500m Adidas deal causes reaction from rivals Inter – the situation

Inter are looking enviously at their city rivals AC Milan once again after Saturday’s derby, with the news of the record Adidas deal emerging.

As reported by La Gazzetta dello Sport on Wednesday, under the new agreement Adidas will pay Milan €50m per year for ten seasons starting from 2028-29. This is when the collaboration with PUMA ends, who currently pay €24.5m per year, as per the last accounts.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

The paper (via Calciomercato.com) go on to state that it is likely that the €50m yearly figure includes sporting bonuses, such as participation in the Champions League, the value of material supplies (value in kind) and a portion to be invested in promotional activities (marketing fund).

Contracts with kit makers are not limited to recognising the value of just the home, away, third and other shirts, but can extend to the sale of related products. Then, guaranteed minimums and royalties come into play that are triggered above a certain turnover threshold.

For example, in addition to the €24.5m from PUMA, €55.8m in revenues came from store, e-commerce and merchandising/licensing activities, in particular those relating to the contract with the same German company and those from licensing with Fanatics and MatchWornShirt.

As for Inter, the renewal with Nike – effective from 2023 – resulted in a 70% increase over the previous contract, but the €28m per year is not in line with the club’s current commercial value. In addition to the Milan-Adidas deal, Juventus currently get €46m per year from Adidas (€41m from 2027-28).

Inter have maintained their merchandising revenues internally, over €35m in 2025-26 thanks to the new business model introduced with Fanatics, but Nike’s €28m is too little according to the Nerazzurri’s commercial management.

The contract expires in 2031, and La Gazzetta report that they will seek to renegotiate the deal to avoid accumulating delays over the next five years. Considering that Juventus and Milan have committed to the next decade, Inter have leverage as the only one of the ‘big three’ up for grabs.

#2061. Blackburn Rovers 2- 1 West Ham United | The morning after

Scott Parker’s words at full time pretty much summed up the remainder of this Championship season for West Ham United following the side’s first away defeat of the campaign. The new manager bounce failed to materialise as his squad thew away chance after chance against their solid opponents who twice capitalised on the now-traditional lacklustre Irons’ defending.

Speaking after the game to BBC Radio London, a hoarse Hammers head coach declared :

Not only at Ewood Park, but in the 31 remaining games of this season. A six point gap between the Hammers in ninth and the league leaders is not yet insurmountable. But it is, certainly, a mountain to climb for Parker to turn West Ham’s dreadfully mediocre-looking squad into Championship contenders.

With so many leaks, it is difficult to know which hole to plug first in the slowly sinking good ship West Ham United. Goalkeeper, defence, midfield, attack – all are areas crying out for urgent post-Nuno repair.. But none are yet beyond salvage.

A tough watch – Scott Parker will have learned a lot about his West Ham squad

As many have commented, though, it’s going to be a long season.

Right now, half a season of the dour, drab, boring but solid wins for which Scott Parker received so much criticism from his time at Burnley would be pretty well received in east London.

Usually we curse the international break but I have a feeling this time around it comes as a huge relief to the manager, the squad and supporters, for very different reasons. Amongst supporters, optimism will no doubt resurface at some stage during the next fortnight as we convince ourselves that if nothing else, we have the right man for the job at the helm.

Whatever Scott Parker is getting paid, if he somehow manages to transform this group into his trademark mean, lean, tough side capable of grinding out one-nil victories week in, week out, frankly he’ll be worth every penny.

#2060. 17-pass Liverpool player was ‘virtually anonymous’ v Fenerbahce; it’ll be a ‘concern’ for Iraola

One Liverpool player was accused of being ‘virtually anonymous’ in the Reds’ 3-2 defeat to Fenerbahce in the Champions League on Wednesday.

Andoni Iraola overhauled his attack for the game in Istanbul with a reshuffle which saw Bradley Barcola deployed in an unfamiliar centre-forward role as Alexander Isak began on the substitutes’ bench.

The Swedish marksman came on as part of a triple change in the 66th minute and scored with his first touch, but that goal would ultimately count for nothing as the home side struck twice more to secure victory.

Barcola stayed on the pitch for the full 90 minutes at the Sukru Saracoglu Stadium, but his performance came in for criticism from Liverpool Echo reporter Paul Gorst.

The journalist gave the France international a lowly 4/10 in his post-match player ratings as he wrote: ‘Virtually anonymous in that centre-forward role that is unfamiliar to him. Glanced one header wide. Moved wide with 25 minutes to go but still struggled. This was a concern.’

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Iraola has shown that he likes his attackers to be flexible enough to play anywhere across the forward line, but the experiment of playing Barcola in the number 9 role didn’t work.

The Frenchman was unable to get on the end of a teasing cross from Joe Gomez in the way that a more natural poacher like Isak might’ve done, and he’ll feel that he should’ve done better with a glancing header shortly before half-time.

He did prompt one good save from Ederson after the interval, but on the whole the 24-year-old was disappointingly peripheral, as the figures below from Sofascore would suggest.

We fully expect Isak to be restored at centre-forward for the visit to Crystal Palace on Sunday, but it’ll be interesting to see whether Barcola reverts to a wide role or is omitted from the starting XI after a subdued display tonight.

On this evidence, we don’t envisage him being asked to lead the line again any time soon.

#2059. “Erased” – Media explanation for one star’s waning at West Ham United

West Ham’s Nuno- divided squad was rallied midweek by new manager Scott Parker with his declaration that the slate had been wiped clean and that everyone had a chance to impress. Indeed as if to prove the point his first match day squad included Soungoutou Magassa, one of the summer want-aways who didn’t get his way.

However, anxious voices across the Atlantic continue to berate West Ham for ruining the career of Mexico’s national team captain Edson Alvarez.

Few in Central America seem able to understand el Machin’s fall from grace, despite both injury and scandal dogging the midfielder during the summer. Rather than accepting that the West Ham management simply don’t rate their skipper, the understandably patriotic local media indulge themselves in all manner of excuses for their star’s waning in east London.

Edson Alvarez pictured back in training in Parker’s pre-Blackburn session.

“91 days in oblivion, with Alvarez still erased from West Ham.

#2057. Liam Scales' honest Celtic form verdict after avoiding 'nightmare' vs Kilmarnock

It wasn't pretty and it wasn't memorable, but as is usually the case under Martin O'Neill, Celtic got the job done.

The manager couldn't have picked a kinder fixture – at home against the side bottom of the table – for his team to return to winning ways in the Premiership. Yet Celtic made hard work of beating Kilmarnock.

Sam Johnstone produced a crucial double save inside the opening minute to deny Tom Lowery and if Ieuan Owen had connected cleanly with Erik Ring's cross in stoppage time, Celtic would be back in crisis mode. Alas, the hosts held on.

Liam Scales' first-half finish proved decisive on an afternoon permeated with missed chances for both sides.

The slender victory restored Celtic's four-point lead at the Premiership summit going into the international break, although Rangers have a game in hand.

They took care of Besiktas midweek, but O'Neill's reigning champions hadn't won in the league in a fortnight, losing to Falkirk and drawing with Dundee United, underlining the significance of Sunday's win.

"It was definitely important," Scales said. "Two games [in the league] without a win is bad enough, but three would have been a nightmare.

"We knew we needed that win and can go into the break and refresh. Some of the lads can rest and recover and hopefully we’ll come back in this form.

"I do think confidence is a massive part of our group and it was probably hit a little bit. The win against a top side like Besiktas has boosted us a little bit. There’s kind of a better mood around. We just want to keep adding good results."

Celtic's Liam Scales celebrates with his team-mates. (Image: Steve Welsh/PA)

Celtic entered the last international break following three consecutive losses to Rangers, Ferencvaros and Rangers again.

Things felt ominous, with O'Neill publicly considering his future after the second of those derby defeats.

But Celtic rallied and defeated Motherwell in their first game back. Things weren't smooth over the following eight matches, but as players return from injury, Scales feels positive about the future.

"We had Yang back on Sunday, Jota is obviously starting. These guys are getting back to full sharpness and getting minutes," he said. "Hopefully this will help and we can build on it.

"We know we haven’t been good enough between the last international window and this one. We’ve let a few results go and we’re not exactly where we want to be.

"It was just really important to win these last two games before the break and be in a good place for coming back."

Celtic leading the league was rare last season. Only in the dying minutes of the campaign did they return to the Premiership summit after Hearts knocked them off their perch back in September 2025.

"We always want to be on top of the table. We don’t want to be chasing," Scales stated. "We want to be a good arm’s length from the challengers.

"That is the goal all season – to stay top. It’s important to us but obviously there are so many games to play. You go through really busy spells and both teams will be challenged. But we are just happy where we are now.

"It hasn’t been spoken about – but it doesn’t need to be spoken about. We all know the standards at this club that have been set over a number of years.

"It doesn’t need to be discussed where we want to be – because it’s top of the table. Last season wasn’t what we wanted at all and we don’t want a repeat of that."

Scales scored his second goal in four games against Kilmarnock, connecting sweetly with Camilo Duran's looped cross.

The Irishman's effort sailed over opposition goalkeeper Nico Mantl and into the back of the net to break the deadlock in the 26th minute.

"It took an age to come down," Scales reflected. "I wasn’t sure if it was going to land on the roof of the net. I was just trying to guide it on target and luckily enough it went in.

"I don’t really have a target for goals – it’s more about clean sheets for me. But it’s nice. We’ve done a lot of work on set pieces, we’re getting the ball into the box more rather than going short and I suppose you always get a bit excited as a centre half when you go forward for a corner.

"It is nice to score and hopefully I can get a few more between now and the end of the season. I felt we should have killed the game in the second half. We were unlucky not to score.

"When you are only a goal up the atmosphere can get a bit nervy and that can translate onto the pitch. But I don’t think we were troubled too much. It was comfortable but it would have looked better if we’d scored some more."

For goals this season, Scales is now level with Kasper Hogh. The striker thought he'd ended his 16-game scoring drought on Sunday, only for VAR to intervene and disallow the strike for a foul in the build-up by Mika Baur.

Hogh didn't let his frustrations boil over, instead working even harder and offering a useful focal point in attack.

He earned the in-stadium man of the match award and was deservedly applauded off the field in the 71st minute. Scales is certain the goals will come, even if he snatched one from Hogh against Kilmarnock.

"He’s been brilliant. He keeps doing the right things and eventually it will fall for him," the defender added. "He was so unlucky with his goal being ruled out.

"And he told me he was right behind me with the goal I scored! If I’d known that I might have left it!

"It will fall for him. He’s a goal scorer and a good player. His all-round game was brilliant, he held the ball up really well. He’s just been unlucky. But his attitude has been brilliant.

"If he keeps doing the right things it will work out for him. He has an amazing attitude and that’s why I really believe he will be successful."

#2056. Official: Starting XIs for AC Milan vs. Ferencvaros – six changes from Inter win

Ruben Amorim has named his starting line-up for the game against Ferencvaros, and he has gone with a young team as expected.

Defeats to Benfica and Bournemouth have left Milan needed a turnaround in the Europa League to keep alive their top eight hopes. There are five games left to salvage things, the first of which comes tonight against a Ferencvaros side full of confidence.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

The Hungarian outfit have won all three of their games in the competition so far, and they are 20 games unbeaten across all competitions, so this will be far from straightforward especially with the necessary rotation.

As has been the case for some weeks now, the list of absences is long. Mike Maignan is suspended, while Strahinja Pavlovic, Fikayo Tomori, Ruben Loftus-Cheek, Alexis Saelemaekers, Matteo Gabbia, Pietro Terracciano and Samuel Chukwueze are all out with various knocks.

The back four that Amorim has chosen to go with is Filippo Terracciano, Koni De Winter, Sankhoun Diawara and Davide Bartesaghi. Given that Maignan saw red in Bournemouth and will miss this one, young goalkeeper Lorenzo Torriano will be between the posts.

Omari Hutchinson and Alphadjo Cisse are set to operate in wide roles, and the midfield double pivot is Yunus Musah and Ardon Jashari. Adrien Rabiot will play a bit ahead of them, closer to the centre-forward Goncalo Ramos who badly needs a goal or two.

Official Milan XI (4-4-1-1): Torriani; Terracciano, De Winter, Diawara, Bartesaghi; Hutchinson, Musah, Jashari, Cisse; Rabiot; Ramos.

Bench: Pittarella, Bouyer, Gila, Vladimirov, Estupinan, Modric, Comotto, Moreira, Pulisic, Camarda.

Official Ferencvaros XI (4-2-3-1): Dibusz; O. Nagy, Gomez, Zohore, O’Dowda; Madarasz, A. Nagy; Arzani, Zachariassen, Birmancevic; Yusuf.

Bench: A. Varga, Raemaekers, Osvath, Keita, Corbu, Rommens, Cadu, Joseph, Levi, Varga, Bagi.

#2055. West Ham fans’ furious reaction raises an uncomfortable question

As the Hammers subsided to their first away defeat in the Championship, long suffering supporters, who’d undertaken the 480 mile round trip to be served up a pretty spineless team performance, decided to let their team have it with both barrels.

After last week’s displeasure culminating an Hammers fans singing ‘sacked in the morning’ to their own manager, this weekend brought the players into the crosshairs as the next logical target for their ire.

..With Nuno Espirito Santo out of the job and with Scott Parker just 72 hours in, the 7,500+ travelling fans turned on their stars.

Under no illusions after the result – and the away fans’ response – yesterday: Scott Parker

..As well as booing their own goal keeper pretty much throughout, if the reports on the radio were correct.

Traditionalists will likely be aghast at the thought of fans undermining their own team in this manner, whilst those who participated no doubt feel it was the only way to show their contempt for the perceived lack of commitment and effort which those eleven representatives  of the Claret and Blue heritage displayed.

Not to mention the hundreds of pounds it costs each supporter, every game, merely to arrive at the turnstiles in support of our club. But is it the ‘right’ thing to do?

For me – it’s a no. I started attending games with my son when he was ten years old and however bad it got (it was pretty dire in that season of 2003-4) we never left early, never booed our own players (Luis Boa Morte excepted, I must confess to once letting my frustration with his indolence bubble over) and always, always applauded those who’d put in a shift, regardless of outcome. And I’d not even heard ‘you’re not fit to wear the shirt‘ sung by West Ham fans in my couple of decades’ worth of attending games.

I just don’t see it helping team morale or positively influencing the final outcome. Which is, after all, the point of ‘supporters’.

Giving ‘The Sun’ another gleeful headline to point out our sufferings sticks in my throat too.

But don’t get me wrong, each has absolutely the right to their own response. Just don’t see it helping is all.

#2054. Bayern were ready to pay £58.3m for Rio Ngumoha & may test Liverpool again

Rio Ngumoha’s future at Liverpool could be under threat next summer.

That’s because Bayern Munich reportedly remain ‘in talks’ with the young Englishman’s camp following a failed push to sign the winger this year.

Christian Falk reports for CF Bayern Insider that FC Bayern were prepared to put their money where their mouth is for the teenager in the summer.

A figure to the tune of €70m [£58.3m] was discussed, however, Liverpool’s uncompromising position on the matter meant that an alternative avenue in Ismael Saibari was instead prioritised.

“It is TRUE: Bayern Munich were prepared to pay €70m [£58.3m] for Rio Ngumoha. As we know, Bayern have been searching really hard for options on the left wing,” the head of sport at BILD said.

“We talked about Bradley Barcola, whom they were in contact with, and they were also in contact with Liverpool’s young talent. There were talks, his brother talked with FC Bayern, but it was a difficult situation for Bayern Munich. It was not clear if Liverpool would sell him or not. The price wouldn’t have been extremely high.

“So, you see, the club’s decision-makers feel he’d be a great option for Bayern Munich, which is why Ngumoha is still on Bayern’s shortlist. In the end, they had to decide for Ismael Saibari. Rio would have been complicated, so they just looked to seal the comparatively easier transfer of the two. Bayern are still in talks with Ngumoha’s camp, however, and he could be an option for the summer.”

You’d have to think Andoni Iraola and Co. will be pretty comfortable despite interest from abroad in Ngumoha’s services.

The player’s move to Anfield from Chelsea – which infuriated decision-makers over in the English capital at the time – was prompted by a desire for a clear pathway to the first team and developmental opportunities.

While the minutes are comparatively fewer and further between in the Premier League, the 18-year-old has been repeatedly trusted in Europe, racking up 285 minutes from a possible 360 in the Champions League. With 628 minutes picked up across all competitions in 2026/27, Rio Ngumoha is already well on course to blow last season’s total (1,065) out of the water.

READ MORE: ‘I like him a lot’ – Romelu Lukaku has been mindblown by Liverpool player he could face tonight

The other thing worth bearing in mind is this isn’t a manager throwing the left-sided winger out on the pitch willy-nilly. Andoni Iraola has shown a clear interest in developing Ngumoha into a more well-rounded, positionally versatile winger. After some initial struggles on the right flank, it’s already paying off.

Yes, at FC Bayern, the former Chelsea academy product would likely get plenty of minutes deputising for Luis Diaz in a less intense league, and the attraction of that possibility can’t be understated.

But if the ultimate goal is development and access to a pathway, he’s clearly already got that at Liverpool.

#2053. “He’s Got The Yips” Mads Hermansen’s West Ham Nightmare Goes Beyond Bad Form

There is a phenomenon in sport known as the yips. It’s a condition which seems to affect previously capable sportsmen, psychologically blocking them from performing even the simplest of tasks. In darts, it can become difficult to release the dart from the hand, while in golf it can make putting almost impossible.

In essence, you’re frozen, seemingly unable to perform a task which should have become second nature. And it was during Blackburn Rovers’ second goal against West Ham yesterday, when I watched Mads Hermansen fail to dive, that I found myself wondering whether this goalkeeper has developed the footballing equivalent of the yips.

It wasn’t just that goal, of course. The first was equally concerning, when Ezra Mayers was beaten down the flank and the ball was crossed into the penalty area. The situation required some kind of intervention from Hermansen, but there was none. No punch, no parry, no save. Just indecision and a complete lack of intervention.

Unfortunately, this apparent hesitation has permeated Hermansen’s game recently and it’s hard not to conclude that he’s got the yips. There have been occasions when he has looked like little more than a bystander as goals have flown past him, sometimes appearing rooted to the spot or simply falling over rather than making a convincing attempt to save the ball.

The statistics are equally worrying. Based on the match figures we’ve examined, Hermansen has saved just 20% of the shots on target he has faced over West Ham’s last three Championship matches, conceding eight goals from ten attempts on target.

That’s an extraordinary return for a goalkeeper at any level, let alone one playing for a club with West Ham’s promotion ambitions. And while defenders must accept their share of the responsibility, the goalkeeper ultimately has to provide some resistance when opponents get a shot away.

The warning signs were already there before Cardiff, and his latest performance has only increased my concerns. I don’t know whether Hermansen is suffering from anything resembling the yips, but from watching him, I do wonder whether his confidence has deteriorated to the point where instinctive reactions are being replaced by hesitation.

This has become a huge problem, and one Scott Parker needs to address immediately. As things stand, I would have more confidence in either Alphonse Areola or Finlay Herrick than a goalkeeper who currently appears unable to make the saves West Ham desperately need.

Areola is an experienced international goalkeeper whom Parker already knows from their time together at Fulham. I thought he deserved his opportunity against Blackburn, and nothing I witnessed yesterday has changed my mind.

Hermansen’s performance was among the biggest disappointments in our Blackburn player ratings, and continuing to select him simply because he was previously considered first choice doesn’t make much sense when his performances have deteriorated so badly.

Clearly, there is a bigger issue to address in January, when West Ham will have another opportunity to examine their goalkeeping options. But we’ve only just entered November, and there are still two months and a hell of a lot of fixtures to negotiate before the transfer window opens.

That’s an awful lot of potential points to lose while waiting for a goalkeeper to rediscover his confidence. Parker has an international break in which to make some important decisions, and I would suggest the identity of his first-choice goalkeeper should be very near the top of that list.

Kris Gonzo (commonly known to the West Ham community as Gonzo) is the co-founder of Hammers Chat (established 2014) and the lead video content creator and columnist for Claret and Hugh.

With over a decade of professional sports media experience, he is a frequent West Ham United analyst and contributor for Sky Sports News, BBC Football Focus, and BBC Radio 5 Live. He previously served as an official video and content creator for West Ham United FC during the club's tenure at Upton Park and featured in the official documentary commemorating the historic final game at the Boleyn Ground.

A lifelong Hammer since the legendary 10-0 victory over Bury, when he isn't providing daily match analysis on the Hammers Chat YouTube Channel or broadcasting on X (@GONZObignose), he can be found walking his dog and restoring classic pinball machines.

#2051. Celtic star’s agonising goal drought inspires ruthless online game

Kasper Hogh’s struggles in front of goal have now inspired an online game where the aim is simple: try to make the Celtic striker score.

The only problem is it appears almost impossible.

Hogh is enduring a torrid dry spell for the Hoops, having failed to find the net in his last 15 appearances. It has now been 1,053 minutes since the £11 million striker last scored, against Kilmarnock back in August.

And someone has decided to make light of his misfortune by creating Hogh’s Hotshots: The Impossible Finisher.

Players take control of Hogh and attempt to fire the ball beyond the goalkeeper, only for an increasingly ridiculous selection of obstacles to get in the way.

Efforts can be saved by the goalkeeper, crash back off the woodwork, or fly harmlessly into row Z. At one stage, Hogh simply falls over while attempting to shoot. Even finding the back of the net does not necessarily guarantee success, with VAR capable of intervening to chalk the goal off.

The Celtic VAR denial you can't 'unsee' as leading ref drops unflinching take

Things have hardly been going Hogh’s way recently, although the timing of the game is perhaps unfortunate given his improved display against Kilmarnock on Sunday.

Hogh earned Celtic’s Man of the Match award after producing one of his more encouraging performances in recent weeks, impressing with his hold-up and link-up play.

The striker even thought he had finally ended his agonising wait for a goal with a well-taken finish at Celtic Park. His celebrations were cut short, however, when VAR intervened, and the goal was disallowed because of a foul in the build-up.

The drought therefore continues, but Sunday provided genuine encouragement that Hogh could finally be edging closer to ending it.

After 15 games without a goal, Celtic will hope the real-life Hogh proves a lot easier to get scoring than his virtual counterpart.

#2050. Liverpool looking at one of Ruben Amorim’s top players at AC Milan – report

Liverpool are reportedly paying close attention to AC Milan centre-back Koni De Winter.

That’s the word coming from CaughtOffside’s Mark Brus on The Daily Briefing, with Manchester United and Chelsea also said to be among the defender’s potential suitors.

The three big-hitters in question aren’t the only Premier League clubs keeping a watching brief on the No.5.

So there’s a distinct possibility that De Winter could be making his move to the English top-flight sooner rather than later, if he can maintain his current performance levels.

From Liverpool’s perspective, interest in signing a new centre-back is more than understandable given question marks over the futures of Joe Gomez and Virgil van Dijk. Meanwhile, it’s not quite clear whether loan signing Ronald Araujo’s move to Anfield will be made permanent in light of his superb form in the 2026/27 season.

Either way, the Reds will require at least one new centre-half come the opening of the summer transfer window.

One sticking point for Liverpool might be Milan and Ruben Amorim’s use of the Belgian star in a three-man central defence.

But looking past that, De Winter has posted some reasonable numbers since his move to the Italian giants last year.

It will certainly be encouraging for Andoni Iraola that the young centre-half ranks well for line-breaking passes and aerial duels, particularly with the club’s progressive capabilities yet to fully recover in a post-Trent Alexander-Arnold world.

At 24 years of age, however, it would seem that the former Juventus star is still very much a work in progress. Of course, this will no doubt be welcomed by a coach with Iraola’s appetite for development.

#2049. Parker’s words prove he has so much more to offer than his predecessor | West Ham News

West Ham fans may have voiced their fury as the side slid one place further down the table after a poor run of results, but at least in Scott Parker the Hammers have a manager who understands how it really, really feels to have to witness that dross.

Unlike his predecessor Nuno Espírito Santo, Parker seems to have the ability to connect with the fan base and offer real empathy – along with hope that he will at least, work his nuts off to see a turnaround.

Nuno Espirito Santo was reduced to the same platitudes, the same apologies, but with the sense that it was just for the cameras and that he’d shrug his shoulders as soon as the interview was over, leaving someone else to fix the chaos in the dressing room and on the training pitch. West Ham’s training videos usually showed an assistant taking training, with Nuno either passive or absent entirely.

Even after a year Nuno struggled to convince fans that his ‘concern’ was heartfelt.

Parker has already surpassed his predecessor in terms of being ‘present’. Both his pronouncements and his actions – such as his first-game, half time team talk demonstrate his ability to wear his heart on his sleeve.

His words reported yesterday by footballleagueworld.co.uk do suggest, unlike his predecessor, that he’s genuinely hurting, along with the rest of us:

“Sounding somewhat hoarse after his team’s 2-1 defeat at Blackburn, Scott Parker spoke after the matchabout his disappointment at the result. Parker said that he’d talked about his team’s need to get a result from this match, even if it wasn’t playing the sort of football that he want his team to play.

He had sympathy for West Ham supporters, saying that he “wanted to get three points” for them, adding that, “What I can say is that I’m fully committed here, and I understand the pain, I understand where the fan base are.”

Parker added that he understands that the unhappiness of fans isn’t entirely a response to recent performances alone, saying that, “That’s not just this season, it’s come over a little bit of time.”

And he admitted that he was also hurting from this result: “I think everyone’s hurting here, and tonight I’m hurting because I understand that the only way we can change things is winning”

And it matters. In these dark days for the football club, mid table in the second division, leadership is what will unite team and supporters to operate together and hopefully pull the club out of its slide. Leadership doesn’t always yell, ( he’s done that too), sometimes it merely shows understanding and empathy whilst demanding better.

#2048. Rangers 'flying swan' penalty blasted by two top refs as third backs VAR

James Penrice has been compared to a swan flying through the air as three former top referees ran the rule over Rangers’ controversial penalty against St Mirren.

Nick Walsh pointed to the spot after the Light Blues defender went down under a challenge from Samuel Ramos, with VAR allowing the on-field decision to stand.

But the call has split the refereeing experts, with Mark Clattenburg and Bobby Madden unconvinced there was enough in the challenge to warrant a spot-kick, while Dermot Gallagher stressed how difficult it would have been for VAR to overturn Walsh’s decision.

Clattenburg, speaking on the So Near, Yet So VAR podcast, said: “Sometimes the best decisions are the ones you don’t give.

Read more: Celtic star’s agonising goal drought inspires ruthless online game

“What doesn’t help Nick Walsh is the way the Rangers player goes down. It isn’t consistent with the contact.

“When you start seeing the small contact on the foot, there is contact, there is no doubt. But when that contact makes him fly through the air like a swan, then you’ve got to question if there was enough contact to award a penalty kick.

“I don’t believe there is. Again, the best decision is the one you don’t give, so just play on.

“Football is a contact sport. Not every bit of contact is a foul, we have to accept that.

“Penrice’s actions aren’t consistent with the contact on the foot. That is enough for a referee to say, ‘I’ve got a doubt’, and just play on.”

Madden was in agreement with his So Near, Yet So VAR co-host and reckoned Walsh had become too focused on the contact itself.

He said: “I don’t think it is enough contact.

“If you look at it from the referee’s perspective, he is very well placed and he will see Penrice take the touch away from goal.

“He will then see the defender coming in and trying to play the ball, not playing the ball and making contact.

“Again, hyper-focused on this contact, probably not recognising that the reaction from Penrice did not merit the contact he received, and he has awarded a penalty kick very confidently.

“It is very difficult for VAR to intervene because they will look at it and see this contact.

“That’s not enough for a penalty kick. It’s not enough for that reaction and not enough for a penalty kick.”

Former Premier League referee Gallagher offered a different perspective when the incident came under the microscope on Sky Sports’ Ref Watch.

He said: “He couldn’t have a better view than the referee and, what you said, the defender definitely doesn’t get the ball.

“But where the referee is, he’s got the perfect view. There’s the ball, Rangers player plays the ball, he doesn’t.

“It’s very, very hard to go against a referee in that situation, if at all possible. And there’s the touch there.”

MARK CLATTENBURG: NO PENALTY Accepted there was contact but felt it was not enough to justify Penrice’s “fly through the air like a swan” reaction, believing Walsh should have played on.

BOBBY MADDEN: NO PENALTY Felt Walsh became “hyper-focused” on the contact without considering whether Penrice’s reaction matched it, insisting there was not enough in the challenge for a spot-kick.

DERMOT GALLAGHER: VAR RIGHT TO STICK WITH CALL Pointed to Walsh having the “perfect view”, Ramos failing to win the ball and there being contact on Penrice, making it “very, very hard” for VAR to overturn the on-field decision.

Overall: Two against the penalty, with Gallagher backing VAR’s decision not to intervene.
