#1984. Scotland striker gets ‘something different’ backing in selection battle

Former Scotland striker Kris Boyd has backed Che Adams to resume leading the line for his country.

The Tornio forward missed Sebastien Pocognoli’s first camp through injury but is back for the Nations League finale against North Macedonia and Switzerland after netting four Serie A goals this season.

Adams has fresh competition in Oli McBurnie, Robbie Ure and Kieron Bowie. But with 13 goals in 50 caps, Boyd believes the 30-year-old’s experience will be crucial.

“I think Che Adams will come back in,” Boyd said. “If you speak to Steve Clarke, he’ll say Che was one of the biggest reasons why they were able to have the success they did.

“It’s not a coincidence that John McGinn and Scott McTominay’s better performances were when Che Adams was up front because he’ll work his socks off for the team. He’s a threat and he can score goals.

“It’s difficult being that number nine for Scotland because there’s so much more asked of you than just scoring goals, and I think Che Adams does that.

“It will do Robbie Ure and Bowie a lot of good. Going into the last block of fixtures for Scotland, a lot of pressure was on the youngsters because all the chat had been around trying to get a lot of younger ones into the group.

“But to actually stand back and watch one of the experienced players who has been there and done it operate will do them a world of good.

“Oli McBurnie worked ever so hard in the last four games. But I feel as if there’s just something different about Che Adams.

“We can’t ignore the fact that Scotland have been to three of the last four competitions and he has been the striker.

Derek McInnes says 'gallus' Naderi is becoming a striker opponents hate facing

“With McTominay coming back as well, they all can’t play. So I think finding that balance will be key for Scotland in the next two games.

“Manager after manager has spoken about Scotland having that player who makes a difference in games.

“When you look at other home nations that have had that, you think of Harry Kane and Gareth Bale, world-class superstars. I’m not comparing Scott McTominay to them, but he is that difference-maker for Scotland.

“He is a top player and we have to find a way to get him in that team and get him performing because he has shown that he is Scotland’s talisman.”

Boyd was speaking at the announcement of William Hill as official sponsor of Walking Football Scotland.

The former Rangers forward said: “It’s a great initiative to get people involved from the age of 45. I think the oldest is 93. There are over 5,000 people playing it in Scotland now and hopefully those numbers can grow.

“You can see here, it’s probably a little bit quick for me to take part in it…

“But you can see people coming out and enjoying themselves. It might be that they’ve lost their partners or their wives, and coming out and communicating with others might be just enough to get them through their day.”

#1983. John McGinn stars in eight-goal thriller as EPL record broken while Scott McTominay rescued by bizarre goal

Scotland international John McGinn warmed up for this week’s Nations League fixtures by playing a major role in Aston Villa’s thrilling 4-4 draw with Manchester United on Sunday afternoon, but left fuming after two dramatic late goals denied them a vital win.

McGinn, 31, helped his side get off to a perfect start at Old Trafford, assisting Alysson's opening goal in the first minute, before Nicolas Jackson added a second just three minutes later. A penalty from Bruno Fernandes (16) and a Youri Tielemans strike (44) levelled the scores before half-time, though.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

However, the away side took the lead once again just three minutes after the restart when McGinn buried his penalty beyond Senne Lammens, and it looked like Villa had sealed the win when Leon Goretzka scored his first goal for the club in the 53rd minute. Dramatically, though, Manchester United somehow stole a point with two injury-time strikes from Joshua Zirkzee and Patrick Dorgu.

Having been just seconds away from breaking a run of three games without a win, McGinn was left hugely frustrated as he lamented Villa’s late collapse. “We have to manage these moments better,” McGinn told Match of the Day. “Not a lot of teams will come here 2-0 and give goals away. We have to defend better in those positions. In the last 10 minutes of each half, we have to manage better.

“We have a lot of inexperienced players but a lot of talent, and that's why we score goals. It doesn't matter if United are low on confidence; you're always up against it. We lost two points. We threw it away. The last five minutes were just madness. It's going to sting. The manager is a winner; he'll be hurting the way we are. We go play international football but he'll dwell on it for two weeks.”

The thrilling draw means McGinn’s side are winless since their 2-1 triumph over Manchester City on October 24, leaving them in 10th place in the English Premier League. Meanwhile, their hosts are now the only side in the league to have won just one game this season, leaving them in 18th place and amongst the relegation spots as pressure mounts on head coach Michael Carrick.

However, United did set a little piece of history during the chaotic 4-4 draw with Unai Emery’s side, as they became the first team in English Premier League history to trail by two goals on two separate occasions within a single match and successfully fight back to level the score both times.

Elsewhere, McGinn’s international teammate Scott McTominay saw his Napoli side rescue a point against top of the table Lazio at the Diego Armando Maradona Stadium thanks to an own goal in the second half. The Partenopei currently occupy 10th place in the Serie A after losing four of their opening 11 games, and looked set to fall to a fifth defeat when their unbeaten visitors took the lead through Davide Fratessi after 28 minutes.

Napoli took a share of the spoils though in strange circumstances when substitute Alfonso Pedraza smashed beyond his own goalkeeper while under pressure from McTominay just three minutes after being introduced as a half-time substitute. Already 14 points behind the league leaders, pressure is mounting on head coach Massimiliano Allegri, but remained defiant after the stalemate.

“Let us remember we are not out of Serie A, the Coppa Italia or the Champions League yet," said Allegri. “There are difficult moments over the course of a campaign. I believe we need to deal with them in a spirit of calm. When we are in the middle of the storm, we manage to get the boat to shore somehow.

Bridges were desperate to get points on the board, but perhaps even more importantly, to rediscover the battling spirit that had been missing during last week's disappointing performance away at Maldon & Tiptree.

Jamie Crellin's men responded positively, showing plenty of fight and determination.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

After an even opening, the hosts took the lead in the 12th minute through October's player of the month, Ade Adeyinka. David Przybylo played him through the middle and, from around 20 yards out, he unleashed an unstoppable strike into the net to give Bridges an early advantage.

The remainder of the first half was evenly matched, with Roberts producing several good saves in the Bridges goal. At the other end, the energetic Villavicencio continued to cause problems for the visitors, particularly with a dangerous cross towards Reece Hallard, whose header from six yards narrowly missed the target.

It could have been 2-0 moments into the second half as, straight from the restart, Bridges put together an excellent move down the right. Velvick released Przybylo through on goal, but under pressure from the goalkeeper, his effort narrowly drifted wide.

Just a couple of minutes later, Przybylo, who had been a constant handful for the visitors, worked his way past his marker and had another opportunity to restore Bridges' advantage, but his effort narrowly missed the far post.

With Bridges short of options on the bench and several players playing through injuries, maintaining the intensity became increasingly difficult. Brentwood Town took control during the final 20 minutes, but Roberts came to the rescue with two superb saves to deny Cerulli and Sears, while the Bridges players continued to put their bodies on the line to protect their point.

There was late drama in the 94th minute when Reece Hallard chased a ball through on the counter-attack, only for Cripps to handle it as the last man.

The Brentwood defender was shown a straight red card, leaving the visitors down to ten men. However, it came too late to have any impact on the outcome, as the match finished 1-1.

The point represents a much-needed response from Bridges, who are now into a demanding run of three consecutive away fixtures in seven days against Cray Wanderers (Tuesday 10), Welling United (Saturday 14) and Dartford (Tuesday 17).

#1981. Rangers hero makes ‘ruthless killer’ forward plea as Celtic pressure builds

Former Rangers striker Kris Boyd would like the club’s current forwards to develop a “ruthless” streak as he claimed they were in the ascendancy in the title race.

Ryan Naderi took his tally for the season to nine goals in Rangers’ 2-0 win over St Mirren on Saturday while Kevin Kelsy has struck five times in 10 appearances.

But with attacking midfielder Kim Min-su still to get off the mark and winger Badredine Bouanani on one goal, Boyd feels Rangers can step up another level.

“Rangers could quite easily have won by four or five on Saturday night,” said Boyd, who struck 300 career goals.

“I don’t quite know what it is because you look at Bouanani and Kim Min-su and you feel as if there are players in there who are contributing.

“But I think in the modern game you’re looking and saying, can their numbers increase? Of course they can.

“When you look at Naderi at the weekend, he takes his penalty superbly well, but he could quite easily have walked off with the match ball.

“Kevin Kelsy is a threat and he’s shown that over the period of time he’s been here.

Kevin Kelsy celebrates with Ryan Naderi (Image: Stuart Wallace / Shutterstock)

“Rangers are creating chances, but I don’t see that ruthless killer at the top end of the pitch that is obsessed with scoring goals and that’s all they want to do. Maybe it’s just me, I’m not sure there are many of them in the modern game right now.

“But I would like to see somebody step forward and be that man who wants to go and score every single week, wants to get a second, get a third and get a fourth, because there are chances being created.

“I don’t think you can knock what the two strikers have done because when Derek (McInnes) left Kelsy out at Dundee, Rangers didn’t look the same team. I thought they struggled at Dundee for large parts.

“So you can’t criticise because I think both of their contributions have been very good. With (Youseff) Chermiti and (Lawrence) Shankland out, it’s important they continue that.”

Rangers are four points adrift of William Hill Premiership leaders Celtic but they have a game in hand.

Boyd said: “The start that Rangers had wasn’t great, but they’ve managed to correct that and they’re definitely a team that’s in form and don’t look as if they’re going to lose games of football.

“Rangers have had a lot of tough away games and you’d expect them to keep this run going. Rangers do seem as if they’re the team in the ascendancy and they’ve got that belief behind them.

“Whereas with Celtic, they’re winning games of football, maybe not convincingly, but you feel as if there’s just a crisis around the corner. It seems to be that with any dip, it’s a full-blown attack on the board, a full-blown attack on the manager and then the players get it.”

#1980. Scotland international celebrates Pocognoli call-up with rare assist but is left to rue 52 second mistake

Scotland international Ryan Porteous celebrated his recall to the national team by grabbing a rare assist for LAFC, but was left to rue an early mistake as his side fell to a 2-1 away defeat against Seattle Sounders on Sunday night.

Porteous, 27, was named in the Scotland squad by head coach Sebastien Pocognoli as an injury replacement for Stephen Welsh at the weekend, with the Swansea City defender ruled out after picking up an injury in the 3-1 EFL Championship defeat to Portsmouth last Tuesday.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

It means Porteous could make his first Scotland appearance since he was introduced as a late substitute in the 1-0 Nations League play-off win in Greece back in March 2025, as the national team prepares for a double-header against North Macedonia and Switzerland later this week.

The former Hibs centre-back added to his successful week by picking up his first assist of the season for Los Angeles FC as they fell to a narrow defeat at Seattle in their last regular season game. However, the clash began in disastrous fashion for the visitors, with Slovakian international Albert Rusnak putting Seattle into the lead after just 52 seconds at Lumen Field.

With Los Angeles in possession of the ball from kick-off, Hugo Lloris’ attempt to pass the ball back to Porteous caused confusion, with the Scottish defender and Mathieu Choiniere appearing to get in each other’s way. The latter lost the ball under pressure, allowing Cristian Roldan to pinch the ball and cross for Rusnak to tap into an empty net to put the home side into an early lead.

The home side then added a second just after the half-hour mark through winger Sebastian Gomez, with the 20-year-old’s shot from just inside the area deflecting into the top corner beyond Lloris to put the hosts into a commanding first-half lead as they looked to get a win that would seal their place in the end-of-season MLS playoffs, which begins later this month.

LAFC did their best to launch a comeback, with the visitors having 13 attempts on goal in the second 45 to Seattle’s zero. However, they couldn’t to find a breakthrough until the 82nd minute, with Porteous rising highest to Leo Walta’s free-kick, and heading across goal for centre-back partner Eddie Segura to bullet home and reduce the deficit.

In the end, though, the second-half onslaught was not enough to rescue a point in the Emerald City, as LAFC ended the regular Western Conference season in sixth place on 47 points, with 12 wins, 11 draws and 11 defeats, setting up a round of 16 clash with St. Louis City in the MLS playoffs on November 23.

“Conceding a goal inside the first minute completely changes the game plan,” lamented LAFC defender Segura. “We can't keep putting ourselves in a position where we are chasing matches from the opening whistle. It is a bad habit we have to fix immediately before the playoffs start.”

The sloppy goals conceded are a clear reflection of everything that went wrong, with individual errors and an attitude that’s hard to explain, especially after the resounding win against Inter in the derby just a few days ago.

According to MilanNews, Amorim gave a long speech to the team in the dressing room after the match. There was a face-to-face discussion about this disappointing defeat and how it came about, including the wrong approach and numerous shortcomings in the overall management of the match.

It came after Amorim had given his thoughts on the game to Sky, speaking about a lack of desire and concentration, and about how he could not defend a performance like that despite normally going to bat for his players. A response is needed in Genoa on Sunday, or it could be a bitter break.

In the changing room he held everyone – including himself – accountable. The Portuguese also touched on some points that have been reiterated cyclically by various coaches since the post-Scudetto season.

Among these is the fact that Milan carry greater responsibilities than other clubs and that wearing the Rossoneri shirt is not a prize, but rather a new step in everyone’s career. The reference to how Strahinja Pavlovic trains was emblematic in identifying the Serbian as the standard to follow.

Obviously, Gerry Cardinale also wasn’t happy with the defeat against Ferencvaros, which comes after the derby victory and four days of work that made it even more emotionally impactful. The Milan owner is expected to return to Italy for Genoa-Milan on Sunday, and intends to further investigate the team’s ups and downs.

#1978. Ref watch: Dermot Gallagher makes telling Brentford and Igor Thiago observation after red card at Brighton

Former Premier League referee Dermot Gallagher believes Igor Thiago's red card in the 2-0 loss at Brighton was ”not a terrible decision.”

Brentford striker Thiago was initially shown a yellow card by referee Michael Oliver after reacting to a shirt pull and subsequent push from Albion midfielder Chema Andres, who was also booked.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

But the punishment was upgraded to red on review as match official Oliver deemed the Brazil international used “force” to push his opponent in the face with a raised arm.

Brentford were already trailing at the time of Thiago’s sending-off following a stunning long-range opener from Brighton midfielder Diego Gomez.

Pascal Gross doubled Albion’s lead with a 42nd-minute penalty awarded for Keane Lewis-Potter’s shirt pull on Luka Vuskovic.

Gallagher, speaking on Sky Sports Ref Watch, said: "I'll be saying to players, this is what referees are doing.

“This is how they're acting, why put yourself in this position? We've had three [incidents like this] over the last few weeks.

“I said, don't give the referee a decision today.”

Fellow Ref Watch pundit Jay Bothroyd then chipped in: “I'm sorry, first of all, the [Brighton] defender [Chema] has initiated that whole incident, right? He's caused that incident.

“When I look at that, to me, Thiago's just trying to strike him off. His arm has brushed up his shirt and hit him in the face.

“You can't give red cards for that. I'm sorry. You just can't. That is a terrible decision to make.”

Gallagher though backed Oliver as he was working within the rules. He responded: “It's a wrong decision. I'll accept that, a wrong decision.

“Not a terrible decision, because the referees have asked. I get that you think it's wrong, but it's not a terrible decision.”

Meanwhile, Brentford boss Keith Andrews questioned the use of VAR in the Premier League after the Thiago incident.

“I’m struggling to believe in this day and age where we see the referee’s call on pitch and the bar of where they’re given the licence to referee in-game, which is what I should think it should be, but he’s been sent to the screen,” he said.

“We play on the edge, we’re a team that likes to play on the edge, I want us to be on the edge. But it clearly cost us.”

#1975. I witnessed recurring Celtic Remembrance Sunday embarrassment but Green Brigade act commended

Despite some rocky results, Celtic have made it to another international break still in front of Rangers. They are four points clear of the second-placed Ibrox side, who have a game in hand, after a narrow 1-0 Remembrance Sunday win over Kilmarnock.

Parkhead is unlike most places in the United Kingdom on Remembrance Sunday. Before kick-off, as fans milled around outside the stadium, there was barely a single poppy visible.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

This was the 13th time since 1974, when Celtic first played a Sunday fixture, that they have been in action on Remembrance Sunday itself, the fifth time at home.

People wondered beforehand what would happen and whether a period of silence would be attempted at all. After all, when Celtic published their Kilmarnock matchday guide, including “everything you need to know about the game”, there was no mention of the day’s significance. All it advised was that supporters should be in their seat for the 4pm kick-off – put back due to Remembrance Sunday activities in Glasgow - to “make some noise for the Bhoys”. Well, many certainly managed this.

The Tannoy announcer stated there would be “some moments” of silence to commemorate the war dead. The Green Brigade opted to stay outside, which is to be commended. They clearly took the view that if others wished to take part in the tribute, then they could.

However, so many elsewhere in the stadium reacted by booing and jeering once John Beaton had blown his whistle to signal the start of the tribute that the referee swiftly ended. The ‘tribute’ was timed at just 13 seconds, which is some way short of the minute that is the norm on such occasions.

To be fair, the announcer had said the plan was for a "few moments’ silence" rather than a full minute. But there was barely even a few moments’ worth.

One wonders if Beaton had been given a recommendation by the authorities to wrap things up as quickly as possible if the booing started, because he did so almost immediately. Although it was an ugly cacophony, maybe it might have been better if he had just stood his ground and let it play out.

Others might argue it would have been better if the silence had not been scheduled – or attempted – at all. Everyone knew what was going to happen.

But then what about the Celtic fans who do wish to pay their respects – and there were plenty. And the Kilmarnock fans, small group though they were, had every right to expect to be able to stand and remember relatives who had made the greatest sacrifice.

The Green Brigade stayed away, which was fair enough. But many inside the ground, according to testimonies on Facebook and elsewhere, explained that they had wanted to observe a silence. The Celtic board have enough on their plate without seeking more aggravation. They are probably just happy that it's all over for another year. However, the vexed question of war remembrance is a recurring issue that embarrasses the club annually.

The issue of Kasper Hogh’s Parkhead goal drought dominated the post-match debate as did Mika Baur’s worrying ankle injury. So focus was not necessarily on the Parkhead return of Luke McCowan, whom many once wondered if they might ever see in a Celtic shirt again.

He was sent on in the dying minutes against Falkirk last weekend when Celtic were in dire straits. The stakes were higher this time. He replaced Benjamin Nygren with eight minutes left, and with Celtic desperate to hold on to a 1-0 lead. It was his first home appearance for Celtic since being taken off at half-time against Rangers on 20 September. You just can’t keep a good (Celtic) man down.

Some questioned whether he could ever recover from his disastrous cameo appearance against LASK in August as Celtic tumbled out of Champions League qualifying at the hands of their Austrian opponents.

After a few weeks in purdah, he started the league clash against Rangers just before the last international break. It didn’t go well. The midfielder was replaced at half time with Celtic trailing 1-0.

Might this stand as McCowan’s last appearance? Again, many assumed so. Tony Docherty, his former Dundee manager and now in charge of the Scotland Under-21s, recently mentioned on a podcast that the player was “having a tough time” having been bombed out of the squad completely.

However, the boyhood Celtic fan isn’t giving up on his Celtic career, that’s clear. Just as Hogh received warm applause when he left the field after 70 minutes, McCowan was greeted with similar when he was announced as coming on.

Admittedly, you feared for him slightly. Celtic were still hanging on to a 1-0 lead and it was getting increasingly nervy. One misplaced pass could have had dire consequence. But he was tidy and busy, and he even saw an effort slip through Nico Mantl’s fingers and into the net, although the whistle had already blown for a foul. Fans cheered, possibly slightly cruelly.

Who knows what it means for his Celtic future? Martin O’Neill didn’t broach the subject of McCowan specifically afterwards but he was asked about an unusual looking squad, which featured just one- goalkeeper Sam Johnstone - of the six late summer transfer deadline day acquisitions. Haissem Hassan, meanwhile, was a glaring omission. On this subject, O’Neill explained, slightly mysteriously, that it was all to do with squad “manoeuvring”.

#1974. Scotland given major boost as key midfielder extends 120-day exile ahead of Nations League fixture

Scotland have been handed a major boost as they prepare to return to Nations League action after it was confirmed that Switzerland captain Granit Xhaka has withdrawn from the squad ahead of the team’s clash in St Gillen next week.

Xhaka, 34, has been forced to pull out of the Switzerland squad after picking up a calf injury in Sunderland’s 1-0 win over Chelsea in the English Premier League on Sunday, with the Swiss FA confirming he will play no part in their upcoming fixtures against Slovenia and Scotland this month.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Forced off just three minutes into the Stadium of Light clash, Sunderland head coach Regis Le Bris confirmed he had been struggling with a problem before the game, his 50th for the Black Cats. “It looks like a calf injury,” said the Frenchman. “But we don't know exactly the timeframe at the minute. It was just the last sprint of the warm-up; that's often the case [with these injuries].

The news means that Xhaka, capped an astonishing 152 times by his country, has now been absent from international duty for the last 120 days. He also withdrew from last month’s reverse fixture at Hampden Park amid a pending investigation into claims that he forged a Covid certificate.

The Sunderland star was accused of obtaining a forged vaccination certificate for a doctor based in Lucerne in order to bypass travel restrictions. He later apologised and confirmed his actions were a result of “fear and uncertainty” and a “deep mistrust” in the vaccine, and received a suspended fine of £136,265 (150,000 Swiss francs) from the Lucerne public prosecutor's office. He voluntarily missed all four of Switzerland’s Nations League fixtures.

However, with the matter resolved, he was reinstated to Murat Yakin’s squad for their final two Nations League fixtures, including their clash with Scotland at the AFG Arena on Monday, November 16.

Needing just a point from their game against Slovenia in Maribor this Friday to confirm their status as Group B1 winners, it was hoped that their legendary captain could return to the national fold for the first time since their 3-1 extra-time defeat to Argentina in the World Cup during the summer.

However, on the eve of his side returning for their initial training camp, Xhaka’s absence has been confirmed by national team following a scan at the Academy of Light after he limped out of Sunderland’s win on Sunday afternoon. Revealing the news via a short statement, the Swiss FA said: “Granit Xhaka has to withdraw from the national team gathering due to a calf injury.”

A mistimed back-pass by the centre-half saw Hards intercept the pass and take the ball around the keeper to score for the sixth game running.

Again the visitors hit back on 77 minutes when May broke down the left, Heath claiming what looked like an obvious offside which was waved away as he took the ball towards the goal-line before cutting it back into the path of Darren Foxley.

He hit it first time from 12 yards, Hadfield made a superb diving save which saw the ball fly high up into the air and bounce back off the post and in – tough on Hadfield after what would have been a spectacular save.

In the final minutes, Heath won a corner on the right which was delivered into the six-yard box by Zac Jeanes to Ollie Rawlins who stooped low to head home from eight yards for his first of the season to earn his team a well-deserved point.

Boss Simmons said: “We were really good through the first two thirds but were just lacking the cutting edge or finish, then in the last 20 minutes the game turned into a basketball game. But I was really pleased with the fighting character of the lads to come back twice and get a deserved point.”

The Bears go to Merstham on Tuesday night before taking the long and winding road to Margate on Saturday.

BBH: Hadfield, Richardson, Holden, Marino (Buchanan 60), Hyde, Peters, Jeanes, Church, Hards, Connell, Young (Rawlins 85).

#1969. Rangers icon Scott Arfield turns to Michael Beale after landing East Fife job

He broke through at Falkirk when John Hughes was in charge, played for five years under Sean Dyche at Burnley, helped Steven Gerrard to lift the Scottish title at Rangers, was a member of the Giovanni van Bronckhorst side that reached the Europa League final and starred as John McGlynn steered his first club back into the Premiership.

So Scott Arfield, who was officially unveiled as the new player-manager of William Hill League One outfit East Fife at New Bayview this afternoon, has no shortage of top-class coaches to turn to for advice about how to succeed in the dugout in the months ahead.

It was something of a surprise, then, when the midfielder revealed who he has contacted since agreeing to take over from the inimitable Dick Campbell in the Methil hotseat and who he hopes to emulate going forward.

“I have spoken to previous managers,” he said. “The one I have spoken to the most and as recently as last night is John Hughes. He has worked in part-time football before so he knows everything about it. I have known him since I was 15 and he has been giving me great pointers.

“But Michael Beale is definitely another one. He was the first person I spoke to when I got the job at Livingston (Arfield was appointed caretaker at Almondvale towards the end of last season). He is the same as John. He worked in academy football at Liverpool and Chelsea. He gave me an analysis.”

Beale, despite being first-team coach under Gerrard when Rangers were crowned Scottish champions for the first time in 10 years in 2021, is hardly held in high regard by fans of the Ibrox club these days.

The Englishman, who is now at Zulte Waregem in Belgium, struggled when he was manager in Govan and was sacked after less than a year in the role. However, he left a lasting impression on one player who became a firm favourite with supporters during his time with his boyhood heroes.

So what was it that Arfield liked about working with him? “His variety,” he said. “I was down at Burnley for five years, where they had a brilliant management team. But it was very structured in terms of Monday to Friday and how you prepared for games and debriefed a game.

“Mick perhaps didn’t have the reputation at that time. Steven was the authority figure. I wouldn’t say he was in the background as such. He was looking over things from a vantage point. But Mick was hands-on.

“His variability and ability to make everyone enthused and involved in the drill was just incredible. His knowledge of football and the variety of his training drills was amazing. It didn’t matter if you were a left-back or a centre-forward, everyone was all in, switched on and really focused on the training drills. That was my lasting impression.”

New East Fife player-manager Scott Arfield at New Bayview today (Image: Mark Runnacles / Shutterstock)

Arfield added, “He was absolutely delighted when I phoned him. He knows you cannot just go in at the top. There’s so many players who have gone from my position and even higher (into lower-tier teams). There’s very few players who can go straight in (at a high level).

“Look at Steven Gerrard, one of the most iconic footballers there’s ever been. He had to go into an academy at first. He was obviously willing to go into an academy and actually sit there looking at kids progressing. He got experience and then came up and won a league in Scotland with the help of Mick.

“Mick was delighted when I called him. He completely and utterly understands Scottish football at all levels because of the cup games we were involved in down the years. He knows it is a great situation. I think I am one of the first to get into management from that core group, so he is delighted to see it happen.”

Arfield also intends to get in touch with Gerrard, who took to Instagram yesterday to congratulate his former charge on his appointment at East Fife, in the coming days.

He admitted there are aspects of the legendary Liverpool and England captain’s management style that he will be borrowing in the weeks and months ahead.

"I certainly will be picking his brains,” he said. “I loved Steven's calmness as a manager. I absolutely loved it. When he spoke, people listened. I thought his demeanour was (fantastic).

“There were so many times he could have lost his head, but I think if you do that, if you're too emotional, players sometimes switch off, especially in this day and age. So the calm, authoritative figure is something that I'll be trying to keep.

“It does not matter at what level you are at, you need to get the best out of players. It is an important trait. It could be the most important thing you have got. I think I can get people on board and progress their football career and their ability.”

Arfield got a brief taste of management last season when he took over from Marvin Bartley at Livingston on an interim basis for the final three games of a difficult season. He was pleased to discover that he revelled in the position.

“I just loved everything about it,” he said. “I loved the chaos of it. I loved getting thrown into it. I have spoken to so many ex-players who have told me they thought they would want it and then when they got thrown into it found they didn’t want it.

Scott Arfield is unveiled as the new player-manager of East Fife (Image: Mark Runnacles / Shutterstock)

“It went the opposite way with me. It just ignited something in me that I knew was in there. But I didn’t know how big the fire was. When I was looking back over the summer at all these valuable experiences - dictating things, coming in at half-time and trying to assess the problems, seeing it from a completely different side from playing – I recognised that it ignited something in me.

“I was just waiting for the right opportunity. I didn’t want to rush into any opportunity, hence the reason why I am here in November. It is the perfect scenario and hopefully I can repay the faith that East Fife showed in me.”

Following in the footsteps of Campbell, one of the most successful lower-league managers in Scottish football history, will not be easy. But Arfield, who intends to play when he gets his match fitness and sharpness up to the required level, is undaunted by the prospect.

“I have never crossed paths with Dick,” he said. “But I have met loads of players throughout my career who have great stories about him. Listen, we have probably got different ideas about how the game should be played. But there is one ball and two goals.

“Belief in players is a big thing. You see it everywhere in Scottish football. If somebody can come in and give you a different dimension it is a good thing. There will be players here who will probably not be able to do what I am asking. They will find it tough. But I need to assess the team. Everybody is on a blank canvas.

“Whether they are good enough, whether I will need to bring players in in January to get to where I am wanting to go, we will see. The previous management team thought the players were good enough for their style. But it will be a different style.

“Obviously I will be telling the players what I demand and expect. But I will still tell them to play here how they would play with their mates – with that freedom. Football is an entertainment business and I want players to enjoy it.”

Arfield is optimistic that his contacts in the Scottish and English game, including at Rangers, will be invaluable to him if he feels that he has to strengthen his squad at East Fife during the January transfer window.

“I remember when I was at Falkirk first time around,” he said. “Yogi [Hughes] and Brian Rice at Falkirk travelled all about the country with not a big budget whatsoever. They were ducking and diving a bit like Del Boy to try and get the best deals. So that'll be my thought process, to recruit the best players.

“The best thing you can give young players is a platform to perform and get eyes on them. Under-23 football down the road and reserve team and B team football just doesn't quite give you what men's football gives you.

Scott Arfield is unveiled as the new player-manager of East Fife by chairman Liam Anderson (Image: Mark Runnacles / Shutterstock)

“So, that's obviously the scenario. That's why teams with high hopes for their prospects give them to teams like this - to put eyes on them and to get their talents growing at a faster rate than what they would get. I'll certainly be trying to use my contacts for the best players.”

Arfield continued, “We've got these Hearts boys (Connor Dow and Liam Walker) here, but they’re not getting enough eyes on them and they’re not growing. So Hearts are obviously going to be thinking, ‘Why are we giving you these players where we could just keep them training here?’.

“There's no obligation on me to play them, but they're at Hearts for a reason. They'll certainly have a point to prove with me. As I say, they're obviously there for a reason. Whether they can get up to a physicality to play in this league is a different matter.

“But the technical ability is there. That's another thing I need to look at - to see if they're good enough to put the current team out.”

#1968. Stephen Robinson sacked by Aberdeen - full club statement as attention moves to appointing successor

Stephen Robinson has been sacked as Aberdeen head coach, the Pittodrie club has confirmed.

The embattled Northern Irishman has been relieved of his duties after eight months in charge along with assistant head coach Brian Kerr and first team coach Stephen Craigan.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

His departure follows a 4-0 home defeat by Hibs on Saturday that leaves the Dons languishing in 11th place in the Scottish Premiership table, two points above bottom club Kilmarnock.

Robinson was appointed in March on a contract until the summer of 2029 following a successful spell in charge of St Mirren which included three successive top six finishes and a League Cup triumph.

However, the 51-year-old failed to win over Aberdeen fans, who chanted for him to be sacked at full-time on Saturday after a string of poor results and performances.

Aberdeen say attention has already turned towards recruiting a successor who will be their sixth permanent manager, eighth including interim appointments, since parting company with Derek McInnes five years ago.

A club statement read: "Following a Board meeting, Aberdeen Football Club has today taken the decision to part company with Head Coach Stephen Robinson.

"Stephen leaves the Club alongside Assistant Head Coach Brian Kerr and First Team Coach Stephen Craigan. We thank them for their efforts during their time at Pittodrie and wish them every success for the future.

"Preparatory work to support the appointment of a new manager has been undertaken, and the recruitment process is ongoing. The focus will be on identifying the right candidate to lead the Club forward and deliver the progress expected across all areas of the football operation.

"Stuart Duff will assume interim charge of first team training while the Club continues its search for a new Head Coach."

#1967. Sunday's Ligue 1 prediction, including Lyon vs. Brest, Rennes vs. Lille and Le Mans vs. Monaco

By Lewis Nolan | 08 Nov 2026 02:55

Today's Ligue 1 predictions involve clashes at both ends of the table, with Rennes set to welcome Lille to Roazhon Park, while hosts Monaco will clash with strugglers Le Mans at Stade Marie-Marvingt.

Elsewhere, Le Havre will face Lorient at Stade Oceane, while Angers' home clash with Nice will take place at Stade Raymond Kopa.

French giants Marseille will travel to Stade Bollaert-Delelis to take on Lens, but not before Lyon face Brest at Stade Francis-Le Ble.

Rennes welcome Lille to Roazhon Park on Sunday afternoon in round 10 of the 2026-27 Ligue 1 campaign.

In their previous league outing, Les Rouge et Noir fell to a disappointing 5-2 defeat against Nice at the Allianz Riviera, while Les Dogues snatched a late 1-0 win over Lens on home soil.

With both sides enjoying promising starts to the 2026-27 Ligue 1 campaign, Sunday’s clash is bound to be one of the highlights of the weekend and could easily go either way.

However, despite their recent struggles in the Champions League, it is extremely difficult to ignore Lille’s current surge towards the Ligue 1 summit, and we are backing them to maintain the pressure on PSG by collecting all three points this weekend.

Le Mans will hope to dig themselves out of the Ligue 1 relegation zone Sunday when they host Monaco at Stade Marie-Mavingt.

A 2-0 defeat at Troyes last week dropped MUC72 down to 17th in the table, while Monaco sit seventh after a 3-1 loss at Paris FC.

Monaco wasted many scoring chances in their last Conference League match, but should find more clear-cut opportunities against a Le Mans side that are a little over-aggressive at the back.

A new era of football at Le Havre begins on Sunday when they host Lorient at Stade Oceane on matchday 10.

The Normandy club sit bottom of the Ligue 1 table after being hammered 5-1 by Paris Saint-Germain last week, while Lorient sit 11th following a 2-0 home defeat versus Brest on Monday.

Le Havre are unlikely to face many scoring threats from Lorient, and combined with their desire to impress their new interim manager, we believe the Normandy side will finally collect maximum points.

Angers can stay above the Ligue 1 relegation line on Sunday with a victory over a rejuvenated Nice at Stade Raymond Kopa.

A 2-0 defeat at Lyon last weekend dropped Les Scoistes down to 15th in the table, while Nice climbed up to eighth after a convincing 5-2 home win versus Rennes.

Nice are starting to find their form and given how strong they are in possession we expect they will eventually wear down the home side and come out on top.

On a mission to record back-to-back wins, Brest welcome title-chasing Lyon to Stade Francis-Le Ble on Sunday afternoon for a Ligue 1 contest.

Les Pirates picked up a comfortable success at Lorient last time out, whereas Les Gones have been busy on continental duty, sharing the spoils at Real Sociedad.

After a positive result at Lorient last weekend, Brest face a tougher test in the form of Lyon this time around.

Despite exerting themselves in Spain on Thursday night, Les Gones should be fresh enough to earn a point at Stade Francis-Le Ble.

Fresh off a pulverizing Champions League defeat in midweek, Lens will try to build themselves back up when they welcome Marseille to Stade Bollaert-Delelis on Sunday.

After nine matchdays, Lens sit ninth in Ligue 1, losing 1-0 at Lille last weekend, with OM now two points above them in sixth thanks to a 2-0 win over Toulouse.

Lens may be shell-shocked when they take to the field on Sunday after that lopsided defeat in Europe this week.

As such, we expect them to play rather timidly, which will play right into Marseille's hands, who are starting to round into form, especially in this competition.

#1965. Stephen Robinson was always wrong man for Aberdeen - what needs to change culturally and who next

Aberdeen have mercifully brought the axe down on Stephen Robinson’s ill-fated tenure as Pittodrie head coach.

The Northern Irishman arrived in the North East to what could at best be described as a mixed response from the Red Army. It was an appointment that smacked of desperation by Dave Cormack and the board, a ‘break glass in case of emergency’ scenario more than anything.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The decision wasn’t without merit. Aberdeen were in serious danger of relegation last season had they not done something and a head coach with Robinson’s extensive knowledge of the Scottish Premiership was a safe bet to navigate them away from that particular danger.

That alone was never going to be enough to endear him to the supporters who had been so vehemently against his arrival to begin with and, unfortunately, the former St Mirren boss did very little to win those boo boys over in the subsequent eight months. Unpopular signings who failed to hit the ground running and questionable comments to the press didn’t help but results were ultimately the deciding factor.

The biggest criticism levelled at the 51-year-old was that the Aberdeen job was simply too big for him. That has always been a bit of a vague statement but his tenure certainly didn’t do anything to prove it wasn’t the case.

It has also been said that chairman Dave Cormack doesn’t know what he’s doing when it comes to appointing head coaches. That certainly seems far closer to the truth.

The thing about all of the club’s post-Derek McInnes appointments is that most don’t share anything in common. It started with a young up and comer in Stephen Glass, followed by a flavour of the month appointment in Jim Goodwin and then giving the caretaker a shot after a string of good results with Barry Robson.

Then came the exciting foreigner with the bold tactical approach in Jimmy Thelin (let’s just pretend Neil Warnock didn’t happen shall we) and finally the safe hands of Robinson which proved to be anything but. Had Cormack been in a position to stick it out and hold on for Eirik Horneland - the apparent first choice prior to Robinson’s appointment - then you would have at least seen a pattern in the type of manager he had decided was what they wanted in the Pittodrie dugout.

Changing gaffers every year isn’t the problem, it’s the neck-snapping cultural shock in going from a Glass to a Goodwin to a Thelin to a Robinson that is the bigger issue. It almost doesn’t matter if the next manager and even the one after that doesn’t work out, what needs to be decided is the type of coach they want in the dugout and stick to that plan whoever it is.

So who and what will the Dons go for this time around? Will sporting director Lutz Pfannenstiel pull an obscure name from the continent? Could recently appointed chief executive Adrian Bevington turn to his extensive contacts in English football?

In truth, they don’t need to look that far afield. In terms of who is out there in the Scottish top flight now, the talk of John McGlynn is completely warranted.

No, he’s not the glamorous name that is going to shift those mid-season ticket sales but it makes a lot of sense. He not only knows Scottish football but he knows the demands associated with a club of Aberdeen’s stature given his long association with Hearts where he also had a stint as their head coach.

Being in charge of Falkirk at their absolute lowest ebb in League One will have been a unique challenge as an almighty big fish in such a small pond and there will have been lessons from that he could take to Pittodrie. He’s got a great recent track record, a sensible head on his shoulders and doesn’t come with anything like the baggage that Robinson did surrounding his perceived negative tactics at previous jobs.

McGlynn’s Falkirk side, currently third in the league table, play good football. That’s not the huge sticking point that most people would have you believe is a non-negotiable for Aberdeen supporters but it does help.

Ask yourself though, if you were John McGlynn, would you trade your current job at Falkirk for the Aberdeen one? At 64-years-old he might not get many chances to manage a club of their stature again but, if I was him, I probably wouldn’t.

There’s another name that’s not being spoken about nearly as much that seems to tick a lot of boxes. St Johnstone boss Simo Valakari.

He’s got that combination of a strong understanding of the Scottish football landscape plus the overseas appeal to appease both sides of the supporters who are at odds over which they’d rather prioritise. He has developed a clear tactical identity for positive, front foot football which has earned him praise and seems to have cultivated an excellent dressing room atmosphere at McDiarmid Park.

Any time you ask a Saints fan or one of his players about the Finn their face seems to light up. Robinson had a likability issue as Aberdeen boss, that’s not something Valakari would struggle with.

No, he hasn’t got any experience with a club of Aberdeen’s size but what he can do is work miracles with a tiny budget and players who most probably wouldn’t have even considered Premiership standard before he got his hands on them.

If they’re looking to establish a brand for Aberdeen managers of the future then he’s the perfect patient zero. A positive character who wants to play positive football.

They needed an appointment last season to save them from the mess they had gotten into and this time around they have longer to steady the ship and push on. They have the luxury of some time to get the right man in, but not forever, so perhaps it’s best to ask the question now about what exactly they want their club to be and who is the right type of coach to enact that vision.

#1964. Worthing Women: Hero Woods is spot on

Worthing Women came from 3-0 down to take their League Cup tie at Camden Town to penalties, where goalkeeper Sian Woods made a pair of decisive saves in the shootout.

After experiencing a dry spell in front of goal at home to Sutton United seven days ago, Manager Jesus Cordon shuffled his pack to bring back the trio of Nicole Mackay, Kendall Varitek and the available again Skye Birkinshaw. Paige Baker-Carroll dropped down to the subs’ bench initially, alongside Hattie Rainey and Ludmila De Sousa.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Facing a side a division below them but with a 100% league record, the visitors took the game to their hosts during the early exchanges. Birkinshaw’s pace took her clear on the left, only for her cross to flash across the eighteen yard box with no one there to convert it.

Two minutes later, Ruby Melis conceded possession to Andrea Chan, with the former Islington Borough forward supplying Ice Kamara who curled wide of the target.

Clear-cut chances proved hard to come by for a while, until Kamara kept her cool to rob ‘keeper Woods and slot into an unguarded net, midway through the first-half.

Town, a team only beaten once in all competitions in 2026-27 - and that was at two-division higher Saltdean United in the FA Cup - rapidly gained confidence. Substitute Hannah Goffi combined with top scorer Maya Brueckner, to slip her teammate in for a shot which was confidently repelled by Brighton & Hove Albion loanee Woods. Chan unable to keep her effort down on the rebound.

Riding out the storm, a red Skye broke out when the Worthing winger fired in a deflected delivery that Mackay headed goalwards, netminder Maelie Rance kept out and a defender on the line cleared away from Varitek following up.

A brilliant diagonal pass by Neve McEvaddy then picked out Jess Richardson in the danger zone but Rance rebuffed at the expense of a corner.

Woods earned her corn once again, courtesy of a fine stop to prevent the partnership of ex-Lewes and Steyning midfielder Goffi and Brueckner from bearing fruit, shortly before the break.

Although the latter wouldn’t have to wait long to double the homesters advantage, as Woods uncharacteristically spilled the ball to present Brueckner with a simple opportunity to maintain her goal-a-game ratioThere was still time for an opening to fall to Annie Gracey in the ‘d’ but the Rebels attacker drove her attempt the wrong side of the post.

No sooner had the second period got underway than the visitors were staring down the barrel of a cup upset. An excellent through ball from the halfway line released replacement Amelia Shiner to calmly slot past the exposed Woods and seemingly put the game to bed.

Three short minutes later though, Rainey, part of a triple change at the interval along with De Sousa and Megan Gates, caused problems via a left wing corner that Sanaa Williams could only nod over the line amid her efforts to clear it.

Not long after the hour mark, a lack of bodies in the box cost the travelling Reds a go at pulling another goal back, thanks to Rance parrying Mackay’s long-ranger but with no red shirt close enough to capitalise.

Continuing to apply the pressure, within a matter of seconds Rainey sent in another troublesome flag-kick which resulted in Rance pulling off an incredible save to deny Captain Sophia Wickenden.

Then the woodwork came to Camden’s rescue, as De Sousa struck a piledriver that smacked against the crossbar from twenty-five yards.

Shortly after that, Worthing were also thanking the apparatus when Swede Minja Nilsson’s corner brushed the face of the same part of it.

A lowly four minutes were left on the clock at the moment Melis’ high ball into the box was glanced narrowly past the upright by Richardson.

Two more than remained when Brueckner got the better of Cristie Pritchard on the right and ultimately found Shiner who stung the palms of Woods, as the Towners looked to seal their passage through to the next round.

Most people thought it was all over, only for Makcay’s sighter from distance to create concern for the previously unflappable Rance. The Camden Cat caught out and unable to prevent the ball creeping over the line.

Not that the drama ended there, far from it in fact.

Teenage kicks by Rainey -  and not the Undertones - saw the youth team graduate receive a crossfield ball from Richardson, find space through the inside right channel and even less of it to squeeze a well-struck shot between Rance and her front stick. Queue pandemonium in the Rebels’ dugout amongst players and management alike!

So, penalties would decide the outcome of this second round matchup and, after successful conversions by Mackay, centre-half Ella Terry, Pritchard, Rainey and sub Baker-Carroll for the guests, Sian Woods stepped up to apparently send Worthing through to a third meeting of the season with Premier Division leaders Brentford, by way of frustrating Shiner.

Only for the Reds breakaway from the halfway line, to celebrate with their number one, to be stopped in their tracks by the eagle-eyed referee’s assistant. Meaning a retake for Woods prematurely moving off her line.

Undeterred however, an identical outcome caused the party to restart, thanks to the teenage stopper denying the same player twice in quick succession and, finally, sealing the Sussex side’s route through to round three.

If that wasn’t exciting enough for you, a visit from Aylesford to the Sussex Transport Community Stadium this coming Sunday sees Worthing take on a team below them in the Prem standings by just goal difference, as the Reds return to league action.

#1963. Man United could match shocking 73-year Arsenal feat in Aston Villa Premier League clash

By Ben Knapton | 08 Nov 2026 07:36

Manchester United will be at risk of matching an unwanted feat last suffered by Arsenal 73 years ago when they take on Aston Villa in Sunday's Premier League finale.

The Red Devils welcome the Lions to Old Trafford after sinking to a new 40-year low, having dropped into the bottom three of the Premier League table on Saturday.

Nottingham Forest's 3-1 win over Manchester City saw the Tricky Trees leapfrog Michael Carrick's side, who are now two points adrift of safety in 18th position.

Not since 1986 have Man United found themselves in the bottom three after nine rounds of a top-flight season, and Carrick's side must win to overtake 17th-placed Coventry City on Sunday.

Should the Red Devils fail to claim all three points against Aston Villa, they would not only enter the international break in the relegation zone, but also join the worst kind of exclusive club.

Indeed, only three teams in English top-flight history have won just one of their opening 10 games of a season, after finishing in the top three of the standings the year before.

The last team to suffer that fate was Arsenal, who won just one of their first 10 matches in the 1953-54 First Division, after clinching the title in the 1952-53 campaign; the Gunners ultimately finished 12th that year.

Meanwhile, the Chelsea team of 1919-20 ranked third in the top flight, before opening the 1920-21 season with just one win from their opening 10 games en route to an 18th-placed finish.

The first - and only other club - to endure such a miserable starting run after a standout campaign the previous year was the 1894-95 Derby County side, but Man United are just 90 minutes away from entering that unwanted list.

Carrick has overseen just one win from Man Utd's first nine Premier League games in 2026-27 - alongside four draws and four losses - and the Red Devils are winless in seven top-flight clashes since thumping Ipswich Town 5-2 on August 30.

More unwanted history is on the line for the 20-time English champions on Sunday afternoon, when they could also open a season with just one win in 10 games for the first time in their Premier League history.

The Red Devils have not started a season so poorly since 1972-73, when they won one, drew four and lost five of their first 10, and only once before have they gone eight Premier League games without victory.

That occurrence happened a little over 12 months ago in April/May 2025 under Ruben Amorim, although that sequence coincidentally ended with a 2-0 win over Aston Villa at Old Trafford.

However, Carrick's men are still waiting for their first clean sheet of the Premier League season, also marking the first time in 40 years that they have gone nine games without a shut-out in a top-flight term.

#1961. Why Scottish football must take John McGlynn's managerial talent more seriously as passionate case put forward

Craig Levein believes Scottish football is guilty of overlooking one of its most impressive managerial talents, insisting John McGlynn has repeatedly demonstrated the qualities required to succeed at a bigger club – and even the Scotland national team.

The Falkirk manager continues to enhance his reputation after overseeing five consecutive victories, including Sunday’s 5-2 win over Hearts at Tynecastle, highlighting the consistency and quality of the work being carried out at the club. Yet, despite his dugout achievements at both Falkirk and Raith Rovers earning admiration, Levein is of the belief that McGlynn remains undervalued outside the clubs fortunate enough to have employed him.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Indeed, the former Scotland manager holds his old Tynecastle colleague in such high regard that he admits he would have handed him the national team reins. Having worked together in Gorgie, Levein insists McGlynn’s qualities were evident from the outset.

“I was promoting him for the Scotland job when it came around,” he confessed. “If you look at his record, it's pretty impressive. Raith Rovers and Falkirk, he’s pulling up trees at Falkirk just now. I just think he is undervalued, maybe not by the supporters that have had him as their manager but certainly in a wider sense in Scotland. He has done a brilliant job so far.

“When I went to Hearts at the tail end of my career, I was helping John do some training with the youngsters. Even then, you could tell immediately that he knows what he's talking about. John's eye for a player is pretty special. He's proved that over the years.”

It is that combination of football intelligence, vast experience, a calm temperament and attention to detail which makes Levein question why the meticulous 64-year-old boss has not attracted more interest from ambitious clubs operating at a higher level.

He suspects the changing trends in managerial appointments may play a part, with clubs influenced by perceptions surrounding age and reputation, rather than simply what a coach has achieved. Levein also believes there could be an element of snobbery when it comes to assessing managerial talent closer to home.

“If it was some foreign guy that had come in and done the same sort of job as him, I'm pretty sure he would have been promoted or moved to a higher level,” he stated. “I think he deserves to be working at a bigger club. I thought he had a chance to get the Scotland job. He's done all the work that he needs to do in my eyes to get an opportunity.”

There is little doubt that McGlynn's coaching methods have developed throughout his career. His time spent learning from Brendan Rodgers at Celtic allowed him to absorb new ideas and subsequently incorporate those principles into his own footballing philosophy.

Levein believes that demonstrated an ability to evolve without losing his own identity, explaining: “He went to Celtic, watched and learned everything on top of the knowledge he already had. The stuff he picked up from Brendan, he's implemented exceptionally well at Raith and at Falkirk. He's got integrity, knowledge, he delves into the minutiae when he's doing his team talks and makes sure everybody knows what's expected.”

Falkirk's recent performances have only strengthened the case. For Levein, there are no remaining questions about whether McGlynn can handle a greater challenge. The evidence is already there and becomes difficult to ignore.

“John's got better as he's grown older,” Levein added. “Quite a lot of times, guys who are coming in their 60s or 70s usually run out of energy. That's what catches up with guys getting into their later years. But he is relentless. Every box you want ticked, John would tick that box. I'm biased, I like the guy and what he does at football clubs. If I'm a chairman, all day long I'd be looking for somebody like him.

“He stays within the bandwidth of emotions. He doesn't get overly emotional during matches and he stays in this area, which I think is good for him and good for his players. You don't often see him throwing stuff about in the dugout or anything like that. He's a top manager who has improved enormously in the last five or six years.”

#1959. Scott Arfield lifts lid on East Fife appointment and Rangers mentors he will lean on as Steven Gerrard reacts

The wisdom of anyone with ambition picking Bayview as a platform is spelled out to them as soon as they walk in through the front door of East Fife’s stadium.

The club wasted little time jumping on the fact Mikel Oyarzabal once featured in a friendly at Methil when the Spaniard became a world champion this summer. “Methil to the Mundial” runs the heading above two photographs in the reception area. One is of a then teenage Oyarzabal appearing for Real Sociedad in a friendly against St Johnstone played at the stadium in 2015. The other is the striker lifting the World Cup after the 1-0 victory over Argentina in New Jersey.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

"Choose Methil, conquer the world" is the less than subliminal message, one that is surely appealing to a young go-ahead manager such as Scott Arfield. East Fife have returned to a modus operandi stretching back to their late 1940s glory years of giving bright young coaches a chance.

Like then, when the 36-year-old Scot Symon was recruited, Arfield is a former Rangers player still in his 30s who is desperate to take his first steps in management.

The landscape is rather different now although East Fife has continued to be a fertile place for budding young managers, Gary Naysmith among them. One of his Scotland jerseys hangs in the Legends Lounge, on which Naysmith has written: “To East Fife FC, Thank you for my first managerial role”. Maybe in time Arfield, who played 20 times for Canada, will gift one of his old international shirts if he goes on to bigger and better things.

Right now he is simply concentrating on learning his new players’ names and getting himself match fit. The 38-year-old’s last match as a player was towards the end of last season for Livingston against Aberdeen. Arfield took over as manager on a caretaker basis following Marvin Bartley’s departure and restricted himself to a watching role.

This won’t happen at East Fife, although he will require a few weeks to get up to speed. The League One club, currently sitting sixth, have bagged a very decent player into the bargain. This wasn’t the case when they appointed his predecessor Dick Campbell, who was 70 at the time.

Slightly surprisingly, Arfield has never met his legendary predecessor. “I have never crossed paths with Dick,” he said. “He is the one figure I did want to come across and didn’t.

“I have met loads of players throughout my career who have great stories about him. Listen, we have probably got different ideas about how the game should be played. But there is one ball and two goals…”

That’s not to say Arfield has something against those perceived to be from the old school. One of his mentors, who he says he still speaks to regularly, is John Hughes, who was manager when Arfield was breaking through with Falkirk. “I have known him since I was 15 and he is giving me great pointers,” he says. “He has worked in part-time football and so knows everything about it.”

This is clearly one of the challenges facing Arfield and all those like him who take a perceived backwards step into the part-time environment in order to go forward.

“That is something I spoke to part-time managers and ex-teammates about who have gone into management,” he says. “Boys have got jobs. This is a hobby. I don’t expect them to purely and utterly dedicate their lives like I have done for the last 20 years.”

But he does expect a degree of professionalism, something he will be bringing despite the inevitable frustrations of training just twice a week.

Four teams maintain close to full-time operations in League One, meaning East Fife must overachieve to prosper. Arfield is enthused by this challenge as well as by getting his boots back on. Agreeing to also play wasn't a stipulation for him getting the job. “There wasn’t any demand on it,” he says. “Any time I have been interviewed I have always said that I always want to continue playing. If you are playing, you are closer to the action.”

East Fife chairman Liam Anderson hailed the “massive appointment” for the club, and it’s true: not many teams at this level can claim to have a European finalist in the dugout.

Arfield came on as a sub for Rangers against Eintracht Frankfurt in the Europa League final in 2022, scoring a penalty in the shootout defeat. He aims to speak to Steven Gerrard, who signed him for Rangers, before too long but has already had plenty of support from Michael Beale, who followed Gerrard to Aston Villa before succeeding Giovanni van Bronckhorst at Ibrox.

“I certainly will be picking his (Gerrard’s) brains,” he says. “I loved Steven's calmness as a manager. I loved it. When he spoke, people listened.” Beale, who is currently fighting for his job at Belgian club Zulte Waregem, was one of Arfield’s first ports of call.

“‘Mick’, who perhaps didn’t have the reputation at the time, was very hands on,” he says. “Steven was more in the background, an authority figure.”

Beale was “delighted” when Arfield phoned to tell him the news. “He knows you cannot just go in at the top. Look at Steven Gerrard, one of the most iconic footballers there’s been.

“He has to go into an academy before coming up and winning a league in Scotland with the help of someone like Mick. He (Beale) knows it is a great situation. I think I am one of the first to get into management from that (Rangers) core group. He is delighted to see it happen.”

Whether Gerrard, who met up with Arfield at a recent Old Firm clash and slightly surreally commented “Yes Scotty lad” on an East Fife Instagram post announcing his appointment, takes in a game in Methil in the near future remains to be seen. He might be barred entry: World Cup winners only.

#1958. Crystal Palace vs. Liverpool: Andoni Iraola could match Sir Alex Ferguson, Jose Mourinho in Premier League fixture

By Ben Knapton | 08 Nov 2026 07:58, Last updated: 08 Nov 2026 08:03

Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola could match a terrific Sir Alex Ferguson and Jose Mourinho record in Sunday's Premier League battle with Crystal Palace.

The Reds head to Selhurst Park looking to avoid a third straight defeat in all tournaments, having gone down to Arsenal and Fenerbahce already this month.

Iraola oversaw five straight victories before his two recent setbacks, and he has been warned that he faces unwanted Arne Slot comparisons if he fails to lead Liverpool to victory in the capital.

However, the former Bournemouth boss has overseen an extraordinary run of away matches both with the Cherries and the Reds, who are still unbeaten on the road in the 2026-27 Premier League.

Liverpool have won three and drawn one of their four top-flight away games, while Iraola is incredibly unbeaten in Premier League away matches throughout the entirety of 2026.

The Spaniard has not lost a top-flight contest on the road since December 2025, when his Bournemouth side were slain by Brentford, and he has since gone 13 without defeat on rival territory.

Should Liverpool take at least a point home from Selhurst Park, Iraola would equal the away unbeaten runs of Alex Ferguson (14 in 1999), Jose Mourinho (14 in 2005) in Premier League road matches in a single calendar year.

However, Iraola would not match the outright record for consecutive Premier League away games without defeat in one calendar year, as Ole Gunnar Solskjaer's Manchester United avoided losing in 15 successive top-flight road matches in 2021.

After opening the campaign with a 2-2 draw at Newcastle United, Liverpool have won their last three Premier League matches outside Anfield, overcoming Ipswich Town, Bournemouth and nine-man Brentford.

It has been over two years since Liverpool won more Premier League away games in a row, as Slot's 2024-25 team prevailed in each of their first four, the fourth of which came at none other than Palace.

While Iraola could match Ferguson and Mourinho with a desired outcome, defeat would see Liverpool suffer an unwanted club first in the Premier League era.

The then-reigning champions were beaten 2-1 by Crystal Palace in September 2025, when Eddie Nketiah struck a 97th-minute winner after earlier strikes from Ismaila Sarr and Federico Chiesa.

Defeat on Sunday would therefore see Liverpool lose back-to-back games away to Crystal Palace for the first time in the Premier League, having not suffered that fate since the First Division days of 1992.

The Reds start the day sixth in the Premier League table, one point below Everton and Chelsea, whom they can overtake with a win if the Blues fail to beat rock-bottom Sunderland.

#1954. Man City are not a team in Enzo Maresca's ideal image yet - their imperfections are clear as win at Leipzig shows they're learning on the job, writes JACK GAUGHAN

Published: 17:30 EST, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 03:21 EST, 5 November 2026

Watching Manchester City is not exactly straightforward at the moment. Downright confusing most of the time. Different tweaks on the same tactical theme each week, City learning on the job under new management.

Enzo Maresca recently revealed that he would rather win games 1-0 than these helter-skelter, drama-filled, error-strewn goal fests but they are not yet capable of producing that. And the players know it.

On leading in Saxony, secured by Castello Lukeba's own goal, Maresca called for Phil Foden and Abdukodir Khusanov to sprint for the bench to receive detailed instructions. As they did, Marc Guehi and Enzo Fernandez engaged in deep conversation. Gesturing arms as Erling Haaland and Elliot Anderson spoke while walking back to halfway.

The body language was as if they had gone behind. Strangely, that might encourage the boss. They know this all can improve drastically in a quest to become more cohesive. There is definitely the talent among the squad to possess a certainty of how to emphatically dominate games like this one.

None of this is particularly different to when they went on the seven-game winning run to fly out of the blocks in the Premier League, imperfections making them eminently watchable but not a team in Maresca's ideal image yet. Not by a long shot.

Later, when Anderson and Rayan Cherki were locked in debate about how to press from a goal kick, it served as a reminder of Maresca's words that this is a fresh project and change takes time. Chinks exist.

Erling Haaland came to Manchester City's rescue once more with the winning goal at Leipzig

He slid home City's winner with minutes remaining after fine work from Elliot Anderson (left)

Yet on the surface this presentable a creditable result, won by Haaland with 12 minutes left as they nestle inside the Champions League's top eight. All good for now, although added confusion comes in how little this could all mean amid an appeal of the independent commission's findings. Nobody is dissecting Maresca's evolving masterplan if they lose in court.

'We need to step up,' said Haaland, captain for the night. 'Keeping the ball, knowing when to keep it and when to go, working together offensively and defensively.'

Maresca himself admitted to shaking up the midfield and back four because he is feeling out a best XI, one he can rely upon and one that mixes that quintessentially City dominance and a more direct attacking line that can punish in a nanosecond.

'I need to understand more things about the players,' he said. 'That's why I'm so confident because I'm sure that we're going to be better and better.'

Coached by one of the Italian's closest friends and former City centre-half Martin Demichelis, Leipzig felt they deserved more. They went behind in unfortunate circumstances, although Enzo Fernandez lurked at the back post to do the honours from Nico O'Reilly's drilled cross had Lukeba not completed the job for him.

And Gianluigi Donnarumma was offering encouragement, almost embarrassed by Antonio Nusa's shot squirting through his fingers. Among other opportunities, Christoph Baumgartner curled wide from the box's edge. Baumgartner had oceans to himself amid a vacant City midfield. Anderson had gone to put out a fire out wide, vacating his holding position.

Anderson was operating there alone on the night, not something he has done regularly since a £116million summer switch, and it presented yet another iteration of Maresca's City as he attempts to locate the perfect formula.

Then two minutes summing up Donnarumma. Full stretch to acrobatically tip another Baumgartner shot wide seconds after the restart. And yet, shortly after, suffering one of those moments that are becoming far too common.

In an entertaining game, City took the lead initially when Castello Lukeba scored an own goal

Ridle Baku (right) equalised for Leipzig just after half-time due to a Gianluigi Donnarumma error

Enzo Fernandez restored City's lead with this emphatic header after Iliman Ndiaye's cross

Antonio Nusa saw Leipzig equalise for a second time before Haaland decided the game late on

RB Leipzig (4-2-3-1): Vandevoordt 6; Baku 7 (Henrichs 74, 6), Orban 6, Lukeba 4, Raum 6; El Aynaoui 6 (Seiwald 74, 6), Baumgartner 7 (Nkunku 57, 6), Banzuzi 6; Gruda 7, Romulo 6 (Gomis 67, 6), Nusa 7 (Reitz 73, 6)

Man City (4-1-4-1): Donnarumma 5; Nunes 6 (Dias 79), Khusanov 6, Guehi 6, O'Reilly 6; Anderson 8 (Bouaddi 83); Foden 6 (Doku 64, 6), Fernandez 6 (Kovacic 83), Cherki 7, Ndiaye 7 (Allan 83); Haaland 7

Ridle Baku was the beneficiary of the goalkeeper's poor positioning, forgetting about his near post, and flashed in. Somebody of Donnarumma's standing cannot allow that to happen. He would soon fumble another Baku shot, which led to a penalty appeal.

'It is not a concern but it is a mistake,' Maresca said. 'Before that he did a save that no other keeper in the world makes. Gigio knows he was not good with the goal. He's going to do better.'

City missed plenty of chances themselves before Fernandez headed in a second from Iliman Ndiaye's whipped cross but that lead only lasted three minutes, Nusa slamming into the far corner just after the hour. 'Silly goals,' Maresca said.

City kept ploughing forward, Anderson kept driving on. Ndiaye set Anderson storming down the right and he knew the area to hit. Back post, Haaland. A wicked cross, a striker's finish. Game won. Maybe that's what they were chatting about earlier.
